The **QR factorization** of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns is the matrix product

$$
\underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{A}
=
\underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{Q} \times \underset{{\large n} \times {\large n}}{R},
$$

where 

- $Q$ is an $m \times n$ matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A),$ and

- $R$ is an $n \times n$ upper triangular matrix with positive entries on its diagonal.

For example, the $3\times 2$ matrix

![](images/b7/b71bb9b1dc9aa6d23f2c990052e2e83eeda6000fc64a61ccdb614669d840d38a.svg)

has the QR factorization

![](images/7c/7c5c30e4011efe0ac87f02217dd1f52c6e64658c6e90d22ad8689209badeb1f4.svg)

Let's consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=-2 \\ -{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} &=4 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

It is easy to show that the system is inconsistent (i.e., it has no solution). However, in real-world problems, we might want to find an approximate solution to the system. 

Let's formulate the problem a little more rigorously. Firstly, we write down the system in the form $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\mathbin{:}$
![](images/22/22b8abd4638e579875755f482442cf1dbf89653bd9d396b4a802217e25177839.svg)

We are interested in vectors $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ such that $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is very close to $\mathbf b.$ More precisely, we wish to *minimize the distance* between $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and $\mathbf b.$ Recall that the distance between $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and $\mathbf b$ is given by

$$
\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert.
$$

The smaller the value of $\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert,$ the better our approximation $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ will be. 

In terms of vector subspaces, we wish to find a vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ that lies in $\textrm{Col}(A)$ and is closest to $\mathbf{b}.$
Therefore, $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ must be the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$

![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png)

It can be shown that ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is found by solving the corresponding **normal equation**, given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\hat{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

We'll prove this at the end of the lesson. Note that the normal equation is obtained by left-multiplying the equation $A {\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf b$ by $A^T.$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix $A^T \! A$ is invertible. Therefore, left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T \! A)^{-1},$ we obtain

$$
{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = (A^T \! A)^{-1}A^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

We now compute the right-hand side as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={(\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -4 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\,\,\,\,\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 18\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -20\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{99}\begin{bmatrix}18 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -20\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{8}{33} \\ -\frac{38}{33}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is called the **least-squares solution** of the given system.

**Watch out!** We assumed that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, which guarantees that $A^T \! A\,$ is invertible. However, if the columns of $A$ are linearly *dependent,* then we have to use a different approach to solve the problem.

Let's consider the following inconsistent system of equations:

![](images/6b/6bcdc34077d88eac5ed89d408a1d2525b617a4f427b13433757df918585d380f.svg)

Since the system is inconsistent, we cannot find an exact solution. However, as we've previously seen, we can attempt to find the so-called least-squares solution, which is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\|  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \|
$$

is as small as possible. 

As before, the least-squares solution can be found by solving the corresponding normal equation, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\hat{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note the following: 

- Previously, we solved the normal equation by left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T A)^{-1}.$

- However, in this case, the second column of $A$ is a multiple of the first.

- So, the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent.

- Therefore, $A^T A$ is not invertible.

To solve the normal equation in this case, we proceed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\hat{x} & ={A}^{T}b \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}5 & -20 \\ -20 & 80\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 20\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the last equation by Gaussian elimination, we obtain the general solution

![](images/b9/b93bd5cb988f208eb26115bfaa08e81be989ee79cf3655612c1a0522a5566d95.svg)

Notice that our solution is not unique! The second term of the least-squares solution (highlighted in blue) represents vectors from the null space of $A.$ 

In general, if a matrix $A$ has collinear columns, then the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ is not unique.

Consider the following data set:

| $x$ | **$100$** | **$110$** | **$120$** | **$130$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $12$ | $11$ | $12$ | $15$ |

Our goal is to describe how to use matrices to carry out a linear regression. That is, we want to find an equation of the form

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$

that best fits the given data points. 

![](images/8e/8ec830e3cf6154675487536afc0e09a42226eb83187b90238a0bfdcefeae5b38.png)

Let's write our problem in matrix notation. Substituting the values of $x$ into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of $y,$ we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0}+100{\beta }_{1}=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+110{\beta }_{1}=11 \\ {\beta }_{0}+120{\beta }_{1}=12 \\ {\beta }_{0}+130{\beta }_{1}=15\end{aligned}
$$

which can be expressed in matrix notation as

![](images/8b/8bacbea6990395351aecca8befe779358d57d50f8c14f865d73c2107688fa728.svg)

The matrix $X$ is called the **design matrix,** and $\mathbf{y}$ is called the **observation vector**. 

Since our points do not lie on a straight line, there will be no parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ that best approximate the solution.

In other words, we seek to find a column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ such that

$$
\| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|
$$

is as small as possible.

Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.$ Therefore, the coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem! 

This approach to finding parameters for a linear regression model is often called **ordinary least squares (OLS) regression**.

Pre-multiplying the equation $X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}$ by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible, and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Substituting $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$ into the formula above and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\hat{\beta }=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0.1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the line of best fit (regression line) is 

$$
y = 1+ 0.1x.
$$

The next inner product that we will discuss concerns inner products on polynomials.

Given a sequence of distinct real numbers $t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_{n+1},$ the function
$$
\langle x(t), y(t) \rangle = \sum_{i=1}^{n+1} x(t_i) y(t_i)
$$
defines an inner product on $\mathbb{R}_n[t],$ the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $n.$

Let's consider a few examples:

- The following function defines an inner product on $\mathbb{R}_1[t]\mathbin{:}$
$$
\langle p(x), q(x)\rangle = p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)
$$

- The following function defines an inner product on $\mathbb{R}_2[t]\mathbin{:}$
$$
\langle p(x), q(x)\rangle = p(-1)q(-1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)
$$

- The following function defines an inner product on $\mathbb{R}_3[t]\mathbin{:}$
$$
\langle p(x), q(x)\rangle = p(-1)q(-1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1) + p(2)q(2)
$$

Notice that this inner product on $\mathbb R_n[t]$ requires summing $n+1$ terms. This is essential to ensure positive definiteness. For example, the function
$$
\langle p(x), q(x)\rangle = p(-1)q(-1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)
$$
is *not* an inner product on $\mathbb R_3[t],$ since there exist nonzero polynomials $f(x)\in\mathbb R_3[t]$ such that $f(-1) = f(0) = f(1) = 0,$ which violates the condition $\langle f(x), f(x) \rangle > 0.$

In general, a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $n$ can have at most $n$ distinct roots, so vanishing at $n+1$ distinct points forces the polynomial to be zero.

How do we represent the double integral of a function over a non-rectangular region as a repeated integral? 

Specifically, let's consider
$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_D (x-2y) \, \textrm d A,
$$

where $D$  is the finite region enclosed by the lines $x=1$, $x=3$, $y=x$ and $y = \dfrac12(x+4),$ as shown below.

![](images/af/af0a1a74df8aec0d5189dc2402fc1840c25d4cd94d8861fa06110cae7b449843.png)

First, notice that $D$ is a *type I* region. 
To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/39/39629b33e25aed05bf9a5ca36180f984e7ff8f863c6966d47f60483d672a8af4.png)

So, the region $D$ can be defined as 

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: {\color{red}1} \leq x  \leq {\color{blue}3}, \quad {\color{red}x} \leq y \leq {\color{blue}\dfrac12(x+4)} \right\}.
$$

Now, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{cc}\underset{D}{\iint } ( x - 2 y )  \mathrm{d} A &  = \int\limits _{{\color{red}( \text{left limit} )}}^{{\color{blue}( \text{right limit} )}} [ \int\limits _{{\color{red}( \text{lower function} )}}^{{\color{blue}( \text{upper function} )}} ( x - 2 y ) \text{ } \mathrm{d} y ] \text{ } \mathrm{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{{\color{red}1}}^{{\color{blue}3}} [ {\int }_{{\color{red}x}}^{{\color{blue}( x + 4 ) / 2}} ( x - 2 y ) \text{ } \mathrm{d} y ] \text{ } \mathrm{d} x\end{array}
$$

And that's our answer! Notice that, when we have a type I region, 

- the limits for $y$ are functions of $x,$

- the limits for $x$ are constants, and

- we integrate over the variable $y$ before integrating over the variable $x.$

A set of vectors ![](images/96/969c7c332d8285fa0419e716cad301755b3ff1f9f074ab55798ef7c6ea09b8a1.svg) is an **orthonormal set** if it is an orthogonal set of *unit* vectors. Remember that ![](images/25/257a1924bd39970f89e8a9becbac5a5f260572a7e181dedc91ebcc4bb04b0362.svg) is a unit vector if ![](images/e5/e5ae26b69002c7beb7ee09911c2f5da8f62cd1c4ab687657a7e995d89c3f319a.svg) or equivalently, ![](images/d8/d8b5f1f6c4f3c8955cffeac4e7a4407b0d7a5e26afbf95d87e6dd71cc83c0c47.svg)

An orthonormal set that is also a basis, like the standard basis, is called an **orthonormal basis**. For instance, the standard basis ![](images/f8/f80114a44b31082d68abe17a7d45f60a6455a147a82001ef548eaed69c0c609d.svg) of ![](images/46/4607eb52aa0195587414ef27616970a6b47226a3bb476e944ac079422dc1e1b0.svg) is an orthonormal basis because the vectors are orthogonal to each other and each vector in the set is a unit vector.

There are two more things to note about orthogonal sets:

A set of vectors ${U}=\{\mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}$ is an **orthonormal set** if it is an orthogonal set of *unit* vectors. Remember that $\mathbf u_i$ is a unit vector if $\Vert \mathbf u_i \Vert = 1,$ or equivalently, $\mathbf u_i \cdot \mathbf u_i = 1.$

An orthonormal set that is also a basis, like the standard basis, is called an **orthonormal basis**. For instance, the standard basis $\{\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3\}$ of $\mathbb R^3$ is an orthonormal basis because the vectors are orthogonal to each other and each vector in the set is a unit vector.

There are two more things to note about orthogonal sets:

- Any orthogonal set of non-zero vectors is linearly independent.

- An orthogonal set in $\Bbb R^n$ cannot contain more than $n$ vectors. More precisely, if $V = \{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \dots, \mathbf{v}_p\}$ is an orthogonal set of non-zero vectors and $\mathbf{v}_i\in\mathbb{R}^n,$ then we must have that $p\leq n.$

**Note:** To remember that an orthogonal set of non-zero vectors in $\Bbb R^n$ cannot contain more than $n$ vectors, you can use the following intuitive mnemonic. There are only $n$ dimensions in $\Bbb R^n,$ and each non-zero orthogonal vector has a $1$-dimensional span, meaning that it "takes up" $1$ dimension of $\Bbb R^n.$ So, you can't "fit" more than $n$ orthogonal vectors in $\Bbb R^n.$

Two vectors $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ are **orthogonal with respect to the inner product** $\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle$ in $V$ if their inner product is zero:

$$
\langle \mathbf{x} , \mathbf{y} \rangle = 0
$$

$$

Suppose that $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix with linearly independent columns. We'll now explain why the least-squares solution $\hat{\mathbf x}$ to the least-squares problem 

$$
A\mathbf x=\mathbf{b}
$$

can be found by solving the normal equation
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {A}^{T} \hspace{-0.167em} A \hat{\mathbf{x}} & \displaystyle  = {A}^{T} \mathbf{b} .\end{array}
$$

The vector $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ must be the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf b$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$

![](images/02/024c12b780df0414ab1cf012e5733603fb1167c9533e199c46628d73ad12ebd9.png)

As a result, we have that

$$
(A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}-\mathbf{b}) \perp \textrm{Col}(A),
$$ 

which is equivalent to saying that $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}-\mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to each column $\mathbf{a}_i$ of $A.$ Thus, the dot product of the columns of $A$ and the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}-\mathbf{b}$ must be equal to $0{:}$

$$
\left\{  \begin{array}{l}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}^{T} ( A \hat{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{b} ) = 0 \\ {\mathbf{a}}_{2}^{T} ( A \hat{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{b} ) = 0 \\ \hspace{1em} \vdots  \\ {\mathbf{a}}_{n}^{T} ( A \hat{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{b} ) = 0\end{array} \right.
$$

This system of equations can be written in terms of matrix products as

$$
A^T (A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}-\mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{0}.
$$ 

Finally, expanding the left-hand side, we obtain our normal equation:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {A}^{T} ( A \hat{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{b} ) & \displaystyle  = \mathbf{0} \\ \displaystyle {A}^{T} A \hat{\mathbf{x}} - {A}^{T} \mathbf{b} & \displaystyle  = \mathbf{0} \\ \displaystyle {A}^{T} A \hat{\mathbf{x}} & \displaystyle  = {A}^{T} \mathbf{b}\end{array}
$$

$$

Geometrically, the absolute value of an $n \times n$ determinant can be interpreted as the volume of the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of the determinant. 

For example:

The volume $V$ of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of $A{:}$

$$
V = \left|\det(A)\right|
$$

- Now suppose the columns of a $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ are ${\color{black}\mathbf{p}}$ and ${\color{black}\mathbf{q}}.$
![](images/f5/f593c123eb081da0399e74c665325774758b48c5f086a7475b959905e1de2763.svg)

In this lesson, we studied the following property:

*$\det(A) = 0$ if and only if one of the columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other columns of $A$.*

What does this property mean in geometric terms?

The component $\det(A) = 0$ implies that the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped formed by the columns of $A$ has zero volume. Conversely, when one of the columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other columns, it indicates that the corresponding parallelepiped possesses at most $n-1$ distinct dimensions. 

Consider the following examples:

- In the case of a $3$-dimensional parallelepiped, if the vector $\mathbf{c}$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, then $\mathbf{c}$ lies within the plane containing $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. In other words, the vectors $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{c}$ are coplanar. Consequently, we obtain a "flat" ($2$-dimensional) figure with a volume of $0$.

- For the parallelogram example, if the vector $\mathbf{q}$ is a linear combination of the vector $\mathbf{p}$ (i.e., $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are proportional), then $\mathbf{q}$ resides on the line containing vector $\mathbf{p}$. In other words, the vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are collinear. This results in a $1$-dimensional object with a $2$-dimensional volume (i.e., area) of $0$.

Calculating the circulation of a vector field along a closed, piecewise smooth curve $C$ can be time-consuming because it often requires splitting $C$ into several parts, evaluating a line integral along each one, and calculating their sum. 

However, in such cases, we can often use Stokes' theorem to reduce the amount of work required by converting this sum of line integrals to a single surface integral. 

For example, suppose that $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2 + y^2$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x = \pm 1$ and $y=\pm 1.$ Suppose also that $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and 

$$
\mathbf{F} = \bigg\langle 0, \: \dfrac{1}{2}z^2, \: xz \bigg\rangle.
$$

Let's use Stokes' theorem to find the circulation of $\mathbf{F}$ along $C$.

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

By computing the curl of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

![](images/fd/fd25c80fd757477b724b320d1941c57630ec1c64f36bdb44d4c1c70c526fa2a9.svg)

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-z,\,-z,\,0⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{P},\,\underbrace{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{Q},\,\underbrace{0}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr & ={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2x+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2y+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2({x}^{3}+{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/dc/dcf7ba14ac2c0f3da12efed6d539817ab1708273f5e8e665fdde14fee28bb4e3.png)

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
2\int_{-1}^{1} \int_{-1}^{1} x^3 + x^2 y + x y^2 + y^3 \: \textrm{d}y  \: \textrm{d}x = 0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = 0.
$$

**Note**: Stokes theorem tells us that 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

 depends only on the circulation of $\mathbf F$ at the boundary of $S.$ Therefore, we could have evaluated our line integral by selecting *any* surface with $C$ as its bounding curve and integrating $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ over this surface.

- $P(X \leq x) = 1$ for $x > b.$

In these cases, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x) = {\left\{  \begin{array}{ll}0 , & x < a \\ {\displaystyle {\int }_{a}^{x} f ( t ) \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} t ,} & a \le  x \le  b \\ 1 , & x > b\end{array} \right. }
$$

The explicit formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d, \quad n \geq 1.
$$

Every arithmetic sequence can also be written using the following recursive formula:

![](images/a2/a2d28772cb4cb6078d2fccdca054ec1c2dccf27a5ea0b5972b9ac174eaad671f.svg)

For example, suppose that we're given the following explicit formula for an arithmetic sequence:

$$
a_n =2n+6, \quad n\geq 1
$$

To convert to a recursive formula, we just need to work out the first term and common difference. The first two terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =2(1)+6=8 \\ {a}_{2} & =2(2)+6=10,\end{aligned}
$$

and the common difference is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =10-8 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first term is $a_1={\color{blue}8}$ and the common difference is $d={\color{red}2}.$ Therefore, the recursive formula is as follows:

$$
a_{n+1} = a_n + {\color{red}2}, \quad a_1 = {\color{blue}8}, \quad n \geq 1
$$

Suppose that Katie took her dog to the park, and they entered the park walking at a speed of $1$ meter per second. However, the dog then saw a squirrel across the field and began sprinting toward it. After $5$ seconds, the dog had reached a speed of $8$ meters per second.

We can represent this information visually using a **speed-time** graph, where speed is plotted as a function of time. To construct the speed-time graph, we use the given information to find two points on the graph.

- At time $t=0,$ the dog was walking at a speed of $1$ meter per second. So, our graph will start at the point $(0,1).$

- We also know that it took the dog $5$ seconds to reach a speed of $8$ meters per second. So, our graph will pass through the point $(5,8).$

Now, we plot these two points and connect them to form a line.

![](images/da/da19f0e96ab0a3857cba7be308c633ae43599706d6b8d521b2cf2e1de0f60596.png)

This is our speed-time graph! Its slope represents the **acceleration** of the dog, in other words, the rate of change of the speed of the dog. Using the slope formula, we compute:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle m & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{8 \text{ m/s} - 1 \text{ m/s}}{5 \text{ s} - 0 \text{ s}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{7 \text{ m/s}}{5 \text{ s}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 1.4 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{m/s}}{\text{s}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 1.4 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{1}{\text{s}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 1.4 \hspace{0.167em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{m}}{ {\text{s}}^{2}}}\end{array}
$$

So, the acceleration of the dog is $1.4\, \dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}.$

**Note:** At first sight, the units of acceleration might look a bit weird. In this case, the units were 
$$
\dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2},
$$
or, "meters per square second." However, remember that this is just the simplified form of 
$$
\dfrac{\text{m/s}}{\text{s}},
$$
or "meters per second per second," which is the rate of change of speed.

When an object has negative acceleration, we say that it is **decelerating.** Likewise, when an object has zero acceleration, we say that it is **traveling at constant speed.**

For example, suppose a car traveling at $15 \textrm{m/s}$ brakes and slows to a speed of $9 \textrm{m/s}$ in a duration of $3$ seconds. Then, it continues traveling at the same speed. The speed-time graph is as follows:

![](images/7f/7f28203c4ebec342d5ed6896e6e37ab822b90e13ede0e8e2c02497a65a5857c8.png)

The acceleration of the car is given by the slope of the speed-time graph.

- In the first $3$ seconds, between the points $(0,15)$ and $(3,9),$ the slope of the line is:
$$
m = \dfrac{9 \text{m/s}-15 \text{m/s}}{3 \text{s}-0 \text{s}} = \dfrac{-6 \text{m/s}}{3 \text{s}} = -2 \, \dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}
$$
Because the acceleration of the car is negative, we say that the car is **decelerating** at a rate of $2 \, \textrm{m/s}^2.$ In other words, it is slowing down.

- In the next $3$ seconds, between the points $(3,9)$ and $(6,9),$ the slope of the line is:
$$
m = \dfrac{9 \text{m/s}-9 \text{m/s}}{6 \text{s}-3 \text{s}} = \dfrac{0 \text{m/s}}{3 \text{s}} = 0 \, \dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}
$$
Because the acceleration of the car is zero, we say that the car is **traveling at constant speed.** In other words, it is neither speeding up nor slowing down.

f(tx,ty) = t^nf(x,y).

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {y}^{\prime } ( x ) & \displaystyle  = {( \sum _{n = 0}^{\mathrm{\infty }} {a}_{n} {x}^{n} )}^{\prime } \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {( {a}_{0} + \sum _{n = 1}^{\mathrm{\infty }} {a}_{n} {x}^{n} )}^{\prime } \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = \sum _{n = 1}^{\mathrm{\infty }} n {a}_{n} {x}^{n - 1}\end{array}
$$

Now, we substitute the expressions for $y(x)$ and $y'(x)$ into the given differential equation:
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle \sum _{n = 1}^{\mathrm{\infty }} n {a}_{n} {x}^{n - 1} + 4 x \sum _{n = 0}^{\mathrm{\infty }} {a}_{n} {x}^{n} & \displaystyle  = 0 \\ \displaystyle \sum _{n = 1}^{\mathrm{\infty }} n {a}_{n} {x}^{n - 1} + \sum _{n = 0}^{\mathrm{\infty }} 4 {a}_{n} {x}^{n + 1} & \displaystyle  = 0\end{array}
$$

We want to make the powers of $x$ the same. Therefore, in the first sum, we change the index of the summation by writing $m = n-1.$ This gives

$$
\sum_{m=0}^\infty (m+1) a_{m+1} x^{m} + \sum_{n=0}^\infty  4a_n x^{n+1} =0.
$$

Now, in the second series, we change the index of the summation by writing $m=n+1.$ This gives

$$
\sum_{m=0}^\infty (m+1) a_{m+1} x^{m} + \sum_{m=1}^\infty  4a_{m-1} x^{m} =0.
$$

Replacing $m$ with $n$ in both summations (since it does not matter which letter we use) gives

$$
\sum_{n=0}^\infty (n+1) a_{n+1} x^{n} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty 4 a_{n-1} x^{n} =0.
$$

Next, we need to get two series starting with the same value of $n.$ So, we take out the term $n=0$ from the left-hand side:

$$
a_1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty (n+1) a_{n+1} x^{n} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty 4a_{n-1} x^{n} = 0
$$

We now combine the series as follows:
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {a}_{1} + \sum _{n = 1}^{\mathrm{\infty }} [ ( n + 1 ) {a}_{n + 1} {x}^{n} + 4 {a}_{n - 1} {x}^{n} ] & \displaystyle  = 0 \\ \displaystyle {a}_{1} + \sum _{n = 1}^{\mathrm{\infty }} [ ( n + 1 ) {a}_{n + 1} + 4 {a}_{n - 1} ] {x}^{n} & \displaystyle  = 0\end{array}
$$

Finally, by equating coefficients of $x^n$ to zero, we obtain
$$
a_1 = 0, \qquad          (n+1) a_{n+1}  = -4a_{n-1}.
$$

Solving for $a_{n+1}$ gives
$$
{a}_{n + 1} = - \frac{4 {a}_{n - 1}}{n + 1} ,  n = 1 , 2 , 3 , \ldots 
$$

Therefore, the recurrence relation is

$$
{a}_{n + 1} = - \frac{4 {a}_{n - 1}}{n + 1} ,  {a}_{1} = 0 ,  n = 1 , 2 , 3 , \ldots 
$$

Note that every coefficient with an odd index equals $0,$ since $a_1=0.$

$$

$$
y_c(x) = Ae^x + Be^{2x}
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants, and the fundamental solutions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ are

$$
y_1(x) = e^{x}, \qquad y_2(x) = e^{2x}.

$$
S = \{y_1, y_2\}
$$

 
is a linearly independent set of fundamental solutions.

after:
We now consider differential equations with **regular singular points** and how to find series solutions near them.

For simplicity, we will assume the regular singular point is at $x=0;$ if a regular singular point occurs at $x=a,$ then the change of variables $t=x-a$ translates it to the origin.

At an ordinary point, we often look for a solution as a usual power series,
$$
\displaystyle y=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n.
$$
However, the coefficients in the differential equation are singular at a regular singular point, so a usual power series may fail to capture the behavior of a solution near the origin. Instead, we account for this by allowing the solution to start with a flexible exponent.

If $x=0$ is a regular singular point of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation, then there is at least one solution of the form
$$
y = x^\lambda \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n
= \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^{\lambda+n},
$$
where $\lambda$ and $a_n$ for $n=0,1,2,\ldots$ are constants. This solution is valid in an interval $0 < x < R$ for some number $R.$ This is known as the **method of Frobenius**.

To evaluate the constants, we proceed as in the power series method. The derivatives of
$$
y = x^\lambda \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n
= \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^{\lambda+n}
$$
are
$$
y' = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (\lambda+n)a_n x^{\lambda+n-1}
$$
and
$$
y'' = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (\lambda+n-1)(\lambda+n)a_n x^{\lambda+n-2}.
$$
We substitute these into the differential equation, collect like terms, and set coefficients equal to zero:

- From the coefficient of the lowest power of $x$ (the $n=0$ term, with arbitrary $a_0\neq 0$), we obtain a quadratic equation in $\lambda,$ called the **indicial equation**.

- From the coefficients of the higher powers ($n\ge 1$), we obtain a **recurrence relation** for the coefficients $a_n.$

Let's demonstrate with a concrete example.

Similarly, we can find areas of figures.

For example, let's find the area of the parallelogram with vertices 
$$
A(-3,2), \qquad B(2,2), \qquad C(4,-1), \qquad D(-1,-1).
$$

**Step 1:** Plot the vertices and determine the base and height.

We start by plotting the coordinates. We can choose the horizontal side $AB$ as the *base*. The *height* is the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite side $DC.$

![](images/d3/d3a1cb6fb7b18d3b6e04460077907e6407dc6215249141cc3db2bdf84a59a752.png)

- The length of the base $AB$ is the difference between the x-coordinates of $B$ and $A$:
$$
\text{base} = 2 - (-3) = 5 \text{units}
$$

- Since the base is horizontal, the height is the vertical distance between the lines $y=2$ and $y=-1$:
$$
\text{height} = 2 - (-1) = 3 \text{units}
$$

**Step 2:** Calculate the area.

The area of a parallelogram is given by the formula:
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle \text{Area} & \displaystyle  = \text{base} \times  \text{height} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 5 \times  3 \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 15\end{array}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram is $15$ square units.

We can find the areas and perimeters of shapes if we are given the coordinates of the vertices. All we need to do is find the lengths of the sides and then apply the appropriate formula.

For example, suppose that a rectangle has vertices 
$$
A(1,1), \qquad B(3,1), \qquad C(3,2), \qquad D(1,2).
$$
How can we find its perimeter?

**Step 1:** Plot the vertices. We start by plotting the given coordinates on a plane.

![](images/b4/b40f205f35a7005ac25b59a4d07d1fd36295ca246d40babe79ed686fc280d727.png)

**Step 2:** Find the side lengths.

- The length of a horizontal segment is the difference between the $x$-coordinates. For the base $AB$ between $A(1,1)$ and $B(3,1)$, we subtract the smaller $x$-coordinate from the larger one:
$$
\text{base} = 3 - 1 = 2
$$

- The length of a vertical segment is the difference between the $y$-coordinates. For the height $BC$ between $B(3,1)$ and $C(3,2)$, we subtract the smaller $y$-coordinate from the larger one:
$$
\text{height} = 2 - 1 = 1
$$

![](images/11/11949d94f12d6041543d71717ba372e766509b98f26b42226872c6383b19f408.png)

**Step 3:** Calculate the perimeter.

Now we use the formula for the perimeter of a rectangle:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle \text{Perimeter} & \displaystyle  = 2 \times  ( \text{base} + \text{height} ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 2 \times  ( 2 + 1 ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 2 \times  3 \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 6\end{array}
$$

Therefore, the perimeter of the rectangle is $6$ units.

$$

$$
3^{\color{blue}t} = 3^{\color{blue}2}.

Given that the implication $S \Rightarrow N$ is true, we have the following:

First, we need to find the complementary function $y_c(x)$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
x^2y'' + xy' - y = 0.
$$

Let $y=x^\lambda.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
y' = \lambda x^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)x^{\lambda-2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {x}^{2} \cdot  \lambda  ( \lambda  - 1 ) {x}^{\lambda  - 2} + x \cdot  \lambda  {x}^{\lambda  - 1} - {x}^{\lambda } & \displaystyle  = 0 \\ \displaystyle \lambda  ( \lambda  - 1 ) {x}^{\lambda } + \lambda  {x}^{\lambda } - {x}^{\lambda } & \displaystyle  = 0 \\ \displaystyle {x}^{\lambda } [ \lambda  ( \lambda  - 1 ) + \lambda  - 1 ] & \displaystyle  = 0.\end{array}
$$

Therefore, the characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle \lambda  ( \lambda  - 1 ) + \lambda  - 1 & \displaystyle  = 0 \\ \displaystyle {\lambda }^{2} - 1 & \displaystyle  = 0 \\ \displaystyle ( \lambda  + 1 ) ( \lambda  - 1 ) & \displaystyle  = 0.\end{array}
$$

The roots of the characteristic equation are $\lambda=-1$ and $\lambda=1.$ Therefore, the complementary solution $y_c(x)$ is

$$
y_c(x) = \dfrac{c_1}{x}+ c_2 x.
$$

Now, we find the particular solution. The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation $(3x^2)$ contains only an $x^2$ term, so we assume that the particular solution is also of the form 

$$
y_p(x) = \alpha x^2
$$
where $\alpha$ is a constant that is to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p$ gives

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y_p}{\textrm{d}x} =2 \alpha x,
\qquad \frac{\textrm{d}^2y_p}{\textrm{d}x^2} =  2 \alpha  .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{array}{cc}{x}^{2} ( 2 \alpha  ) + x ( 2 \alpha  x ) - \alpha  {x}^{2} &  = 3 {x}^{2} \\ ( 2 \alpha  + 2 \alpha  - \alpha  ) {x}^{2} &  = 3 {x}^{2} \\ 3 \alpha  {x}^{2} &  = 3 {x}^{2}\end{array}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get $\alpha = 1.$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p(x) =x^2,
$$

and the general solution is

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle y ( x ) & \displaystyle  = {y}_{c} ( x ) + {y}_{p} ( x ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{ {c}_{1}}{x}} + {c}_{2} x + {x}^{2} .\end{array}
$$

We know how to define the double integral of a function over a rectangular domain. Now, we'll learn how to define a double integral over a non-rectangular region.

Let's consider the non-rectangular region $D$ enclosed by the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ in the first quadrant, as shown below. 

![](images/e8/e80bcbaff16282f00e7e3df487d78cfbc51bb2e9660dde5e2fc421cd4d70a9af.png)

 

We will define the following double integral over this non-rectangular region:

$$
\iint\limits_{D} (3-x^2-2y^2) \, \textrm{d}A
$$

To do this, we will use the following trick. Let's enclose the region $D$ by a rectangle $R$ with sides parallel to the coordinates axes, as shown below. 

![](images/21/214db95d949a8658e3fdbfea8f54c0e3bf914c11d9ef88e1ca4264d64d360c90.png)

 

Now, we extend our function to $R$ by setting a new function $f(x,y)$ that's equal to $0$ outside $D$ and equals $3-x^2-2y^2$ on $D\mathbin{:}$

![](images/ab/ab8eed93d71415d810f4c8c9b19d690317769e270805a6925d35f5f0e4c9671f.svg)

![](images/43/43288ccc496832a1a78f9fcaaabb4a5841fc79db5d2082dff7d4177005b61d01.png)

 

Although $f(x,y)$ might not be continuous at the boundary of $D,$ the double integral of $f(x,y)$ over the rectangular domain $R$ will exist. 

Therefore, we define our double integral of $3-x^2-2y^2$ over $D$ as 

$$
\iint\limits_D (3-x^2-2y^2) \, \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_R f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A.
$$

Geometrically, the value of the double integral will give us the volume of the solid bounded by the surface $z=3-x^2-2y^2$ over the quarter-circular domain $D.$

**Watch out!** The domain $R$ must not necessarily be the smallest possible rectangle that covers the region $D.$ It can be any rectangular domain that covers $D$ completely.

Consider the truth table for $S \Rightarrow N$ below. Note that the implication is true $({\color{blue}\textrm{T}})$ in the $1$st, $3$rd, and $4$th rows. 

| $S$ | $N$ | $S \Rightarrow N$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}\textrm T$ | $\color{red}\textrm T$ | $\color{blue}\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\color{blue}\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\color{blue}\textrm T$ |

Of the three rows where the implication is true, $S$ is true $({\color{red}\textrm{T}})$ only in the $1$st row, and $N$ is also true $({\color{red}\textrm{T}})$ in this row. 

So, if the implication is true, $S$ being true *guarantees* that $N$ must also be true. Therefore, $S$ is called a **sufficient condition** for $N.$

On the other hand, if $S$ is true, it is *necessary* that $N$ is also true. Therefore, $N$ is called a **necessary condition** for $S.$ 
However, $N$ being true *does not guarantee* that $S$ is true, as we can see from the $3$rd row in the truth table.

These ideas can be summarized as follows:

$$
\textbf{S}\textrm{ufficient} \: \Rightarrow \: \textbf{N}\textrm{ecessary}.
$$

  

Let's look at some examples:

- Consider the following true implication:

$$
a > 0\quad\Rightarrow\quad a^2 > 0
$$

We can label each part of the statement as follows:

$$
\underbrace{\big( \, a > 0 \, \big)}_{\large\textrm{sufficient}} 
\: \Rightarrow \: 
\underbrace{\big( \, a^2 > 0 \, \big)}_{\large\textrm{necessary}}
$$

Therefore:

- $a > 0$ is a *sufficient* condition for $a^2 > 0.$  In other words, $a > 0$ *guarantees* that $a^2 > 0.$

- $a^2 > 0$ is a *necessary* condition for $a > 0.$ In other words, if $a > 0,$ it is necessary that $a^2 > 0.$ However, $a^2 > 0$ *does not guarantee* that $a > 0.$

![](images/5b/5b0dccacbb0c14d3b7c9a7a69f1cddda6b3a464bb2ae86b95989798d931d71d3.svg)
Therefore:

- Scoring at least $90$ on the exam is a *sufficient* condition for getting an $A.$ In other words, scoring at least $90$ *guarantees* that you'll get an $A.$

- Getting an $A$ is a *necessary* condition for scoring at least $90.$ In other words, if you score at least $90,$ it necessarily follows that you'll receive $A.$

The occurrence of a variable is called **bound** if it is placed right next to a quantifier or lies within the scope of a quantifier that uses the same variable. Otherwise, the occurrence is called **free**.

For example, let's examine the occurrences of variables in the following statement:

$$
\exists y \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, x > 0 \Rightarrow \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, y < 10 \, \big).
$$

- The following occurrence of $y$ is *bound* since it is placed right next to the quantifier $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\exists}{:}$

$$
\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\exists} \!\! \underset{\substack{\phantom{.} \\[4pt] \uparrow \\[6pt] \large\phantom{.}\bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{\text{b}}}}{y} \!\! \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, x > 0 \Rightarrow \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, y < 10 \, \big)
$$

- The following occurrence of $x$ is *free* since it isn't placed right next to a quantifier and it doesn't lie within the scope of a quantifier that uses $x{:}$

$$
\exists y \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, \underset{\substack{\phantom{.} \\[4pt] \uparrow \\[6pt] \large\phantom{.}\bbox[2pt,LightBlue]{\text{f}}}}{x} \!\! > 0 \Rightarrow \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, y < 10 \, \big)
$$

- The following occurrence of $x$ is *bound* since it is placed right next to the quantifier $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\forall}{:}$

$$
\exists y \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, x > 0 \Rightarrow \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\forall} \!\! \underset{\substack{\phantom{.} \\[4pt] \uparrow \\[6pt] \large\phantom{.}\bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{\text{b}}}}{x} \!\! \in \mathbb{R}, y < 10 \, \big)
$$

- The following occurrence of $y$ is *bound* since it lies within the scope of the quantifier $\exists y$ that uses $y{:}$
![](images/1b/1bc62df716ee92fd4b10afaf4855c740d224f4f26e3537f54b937eb134e21363.svg)

So, in our expression, we have:

- two occurrences of $y,$ both of which are bound, and

- two occurrences of $x,$ where one is free, and another is bound.

$$
\exists \bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{y} \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, \bbox[2pt,LightBlue]{x} > 0 \Rightarrow \big( \, \forall \bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{x} \in \mathbb{R}, \bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{y} < 10 \, \big) \, \big)
$$

Distinguishing between free and bound occurrences is important since we are allowed to substitute values into free occurrences of variables. In particular, since the first occurrence of $\bbox[2pt,LightBlue]{x}$ is free, we can substitute concrete values for this variable (but not for the other occurrence of $\bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{x}$).

Therefore, the above expression can be viewed as a predicate of one variable ($\bbox[2pt,LightBlue]{x}$) since all occurrences of $y$ are bound.

Let's go back to our diagram for visualizing the residue classes modulo $2.$

![](images/f8/f84b296319e078df1827fe29dbd15fb61ce0d10cac69660f11d6a96d5c44478a.png)

Any given representation of a residue class is not unique.

For example, the integers congruent to zero modulo $2$ are usually denoted $[0]_2.$ In this case, $0$ is the **representative** of the class:
$$
\begin{array}{r}\displaystyle [ 0 {]}_{2} = \{  x \hspace{0.222em} | \hspace{0.222em} x \equiv  0 \hspace{0.167em} ( \text{mod } 2 ) \} \end{array}
$$

However, we can use *any* element of the class to represent the class. Here are some examples:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle [ 2 {]}_{2} & \displaystyle  = \{  x \hspace{0.222em} | \hspace{0.222em} x \equiv  2 \hspace{0.222em} ( \text{mod } 2 ) \}  \\ \displaystyle [ 4 {]}_{2} & \displaystyle  = \{  x \hspace{0.222em} | \hspace{0.222em} x \equiv  4 \hspace{0.222em} ( \text{mod } 2 ) \}  \\ \displaystyle [ 6 {]}_{2} & \displaystyle  = \{  x \hspace{0.222em} | \hspace{0.222em} x \equiv  6 \hspace{0.222em} ( \text{mod } 2 ) \}  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  \vdots \end{array}
$$

We can also use negative numbers as representatives of the class:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle [ - 2 {]}_{2} & \displaystyle  = \{  x \hspace{0.222em} | \hspace{0.222em} x \equiv  - 2 \hspace{0.222em} ( \text{mod } 2 ) \}  \\ \displaystyle [ - 4 {]}_{2} & \displaystyle  = \{  x \hspace{0.222em} | \hspace{0.222em} x \equiv  - 4 \hspace{0.222em} ( \text{mod } 2 ) \}  \\ \displaystyle [ - 6 {]}_{2} & \displaystyle  = \{  x \hspace{0.222em} | \hspace{0.222em} x \equiv  - 6 \hspace{0.222em} ( \text{mod } 2 ) \}  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  \vdots \end{array}
$$

What's important to understand is that *all of these sets are equal*:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle [ 0 {]}_{2} & \displaystyle  = [ 2 {]}_{2} = [ 4 {]}_{2} = [ 6 {]}_{2} = \cdots  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = [ - 2 {]}_{2} = [ - 4 {]}_{2} = [ - 6 {]}_{2} = \cdots \end{array}
$$

The same idea is true for $[1]_2{:}$

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle [ 1 {]}_{2} & \displaystyle  = [ 3 {]}_{2} = [ 5 {]}_{2} = [ 7 {]}_{2} = \cdots  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = [ - 1 {]}_{2} = [ - 3 {]}_{2} = [ - 5 {]}_{2} = \cdots \end{array}
$$

The same idea applies to any residue class modulo $n.$ For example:

$$
\begin{array}{cc}[ 0 {]}_{5} &  = [ 5 {]}_{5} = [ 10 {]}_{5} = \cdots  \\ [ 1 {]}_{5} &  = [ 6 {]}_{5} = [ 11 {]}_{5} = \cdots  \\ [ 2 {]}_{5} &  = [ 7 {]}_{5} = [ 12 {]}_{5} = \cdots  \\ [ 3 {]}_{5} &  = [ 8 {]}_{5} = [ 13 {]}_{5} = \cdots  \\ [ 4 {]}_{5} &  = [ 9 {]}_{5} = [ 14 {]}_{5} = \cdots \end{array}
$$

Despite this non-uniqueness, we usually choose the smallest nonnegative element of a residue class to represent the class.

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}- 1 & - 8 \\ 2 & 7\end{array} \right]}.$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda=3$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 
$$
A - \lambda I = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}- 4 & - 8 \\ 2 & 4\end{array} \right]} \sim {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \right]}.
$$
So, we get an eigenvector 
$$
\mathbf{v} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 2 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda$ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $\mathbf v,$ the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1  \mathbf{v}e^{\lambda t} + c_2 (\mathbf{v}t e^{\lambda t} +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

To find $\mathbf{w},$ we solve the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}-1-3 & -8 \\ 2 & 7-3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}-4 & -8 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:
$$
\left\{
  {\begin{array}{r}- 4 {w}_{1} - 8 {w}_{2} = - 2 \\ 2 {w}_{1} + 4 {w}_{2} = 1\end{array}}
\right.
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
w_1 =\dfrac{1}{2} - 2 w_2 .
$$

The variable $w_2$ is a free variable. Setting $w_2 = 0,$  we get $w_1 = \dfrac{1}{2},$ and therefore
$$
\mathbf{w}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by
$$

$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$

The **union** of two sets $A$ and $B,$ denoted $A \cup B,$ is the set of all elements belonging to either $A$ or $B,$ or both.

For example, consider the sets $A = \{a,b,c \}$ and $B = \{ b, d, e \}.$ We can represent these sets using a Venn diagram, as follows:

![](images/83/8351db4817ac8b0d2991fe8ef09ee1f2583c84cb772114ef0614a0ef96c96389.png)

The union $A \cup B$ consists of all the elements that are in $A$ or $B,$ or both. To represent $A \cup B,$ we will shade in all the area that is contained within either $A$ or $B,$ or both.

![](images/e9/e912fe53d530ac47245c916bd16f1758df487ded32da88abfab253ed1ee0cc63.png)

The elements $a,b,c,d,e$ are in either $A$ or $B,$ or both. Therefore, the union of $A$ and $B$ is

$$
A \cup B = \{ a,b,c,d,e \}.
$$

Notice that $b$ belongs to both $A$ and $B,$ but we list it only once in $A \cup B.$ In a set, each distinct element is written only once.

$$

$$

$$

We can use a continuous uniform distribution to model situations where all possible outcomes on a finite interval are equally likely.

For instance, suppose a dental receptionist wants to model the waiting time of a randomly selected patient. After observing a number of patients over several days, the receptionist notices that the waiting time is uniformly distributed between $6$ and $14$ minutes, inclusive.

Then, by letting $X$ be the amount of time a randomly selected patient spends waiting, we can model the waiting time using the continuous uniform distribution: 

$$
X \sim U[6,14]
$$

Therefore, $X$ has the following probability density function:

![](images/fd/fd37b3e19aad197ebb7eeabad00fca068455eed8da462a12630134cd7980941e.svg)

With this model, we can now make predictions about patient waiting times.

For example, the probability that a randomly selected patient waits longer than $9$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 9) & ={\int }_{9}^{14}\frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{9}^{14}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{[x]}_{9}^{14} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[14-9] \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 9) & ={\int }_{9}^{14}\frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{9}^{14}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{[x]}_{9}^{14} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[14-9] \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{a+b}{2} \\  & =\frac{6+14}{2} \\  & =10\end{aligned}

There are two types of "obvious" proof in math. The first type is so-called **trivial** proof. 

We say that an implication has a trivial proof if the consequent is always true:

$$
P \quad \Rightarrow \overbrace{{\color{blue}Q}}^{\textrm{Always true}}
$$

If $Q$ is true, it does not matter whether the antecedent $P$ is true or false. 

Recall that an implication is false only when the antecedent is true while the consequent is false. This corresponds to the second row in the truth table.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\, P \Rightarrow Q \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\color{black} \textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\color{black} \textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\color{black} \textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\color{black} \textrm T$ |

So, if we know that the consequent is true (which corresponds to either the first or the third row in the table), the implication must also be true.

For example, suppose $n \in \mathbb{N}.$ Let's prove the following statement:

$\qquad$ *If $n$ is odd, then $n \geq 0.$*

First, notice that our statement can be written as the implication 

![](images/0a/0ae1b2aec3c4c159d2f0abef58d6cb344f24e8c88bea0d93615e4f9d66d35530.svg)

Since $n \in \mathbb{N},$ it is always non-negative. So, the consequent $n \geq 0$ of our implication is always true:

![](images/2a/2a62ad2d251c3115d9737561381b8878964fafe903e7ec38f4453d6fe4d6f9f8.svg)

Therefore, the statement is *trivially* true.

Another type of "obvious" proof is the so-called **vacuous** proof. 

We say that an implication has *vacuous proof* if the antecedent is always *false*: 

$$
\overbrace{{\color{blue}P}}^{\textrm{Always false}} \Rightarrow \quad Q
$$

If $P$ is false, then $P\Rightarrow Q$ is true: It does not matter whether the consequent is true or false. 

To see why, note that an implication is false only when the antecedent is true while the consequent is false. This corresponds to the second row in the truth table.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\, P \Rightarrow Q \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\color{black} \textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\color{black} \textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\color{black} \textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\color{black} \textrm T$ |

So, if we know that the antecedent is false (which corresponds to either the third or the fourth row), the implication must be true.

For example, suppose $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ Let's prove the following statement:

$\qquad$ *If $x^2 - 2x + 3 \lt 0,$ then $2x + 7 \gt 0.$*

First, notice that our statement can be written as the implication

$$
x^2 - 2x + 3 \lt 0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
2x + 7 \gt 0.
$$

Now, for each $x \in \mathbb{R},$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+3 & =({x}^{2}-2x+1)+2 \\  & =(x-1)^{2}+2 \\  & \ge 2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the antecedent $x^2 - 2x + 3 \lt 0$ of our implication is always false:

![](images/1b/1b051780c4dfa42b85c2d6fcddef3d3e1588c2755dc411a3879e1dae912bc758.svg)

Therefore, the implication is *vacuously* true.

Notice that this is an (implicit) universal statement of the form 

$$
P \Rightarrow Q \quad \equiv \quad  \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, P(n) \Rightarrow Q(n).
$$

Let's outline a proof schema (or template) for constructing a proof of this result:

- **Step 2:** Next, we use the *definition* of evenness to write $n=2a$ for some integer $a.$

- **Step 3:** Then, we substitute $n=2a$ into the expression for $3n+2$ and use algebraic techniques to show that the expression can be written as $2b,$ where $b$ is an integer.

- **Step 4:** Since $3n+2 = 2b$ is a multiple of $2,$ we conclude that it's even (i.e., that $Q$ is true).

$$

The only difference is that we'll also need to use the definition of an odd integer. Let's see an example of this.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to find the images of simple objects in the plane under the action of nonlinear transformations.

Consider the square region $\Delta$ and its boundary $\partial\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane, where $\Delta$ is given by

$$
\Delta  = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 1, \: 0\leq v \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

A sketch of this region, specified with a counterclockwise orientation, is shown below.

![](images/5f/5f91cc8b30f9b764021cd84c374a328c7ffb1287a9f0dc6a211a3fadfac2fdbd.png)

     

Since $\partial\Delta$ is specified with an orientation, we refer to it as a **directed boundary.**

Now, consider the transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to \big( v(u^2+1), \: u \big),
$$

where 

$$
x = v(u^2+1), \qquad y = u.
$$

Our task is to find the image of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T.$ 

First, note the following:

- It's easy to check that $\mathbf T$ has no critical points in the *interior* of $\Delta$ (we'll discuss why this matters shortly).

- Since $\Delta$'s interior contains no critical points, we only need to find the image of its boundary $\partial \Delta.$

- To find the image of $\partial \Delta,$ we parametrize each *directed* edge and map them individually onto the $xy$-plane.

Let's now map each directed edge of $\partial\Delta$ to the $xy$-plane:

- Consider the image of the side $S_1,$ where we have $v = 0$ and $0 \leq u \leq 1.$ Substituting $v = 0$ into our transformation equations, we obtain
$$
\begin{array}{rlr}\displaystyle ( x , y ) & \displaystyle  = \mathbf{T} ( u , v ) & \displaystyle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( v ( {u}^{2} + 1 ) , \hspace{0.167em} u ) & \displaystyle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( 0 ( {u}^{2} + 1 ) , \hspace{0.167em} u ) & \displaystyle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( 0 , \hspace{0.167em} u ) , & \displaystyle 0 \le  u \le  1.\end{array}
$$
So, the image of $S_1$ can be parametrized by
$$
x = 0, \qquad y= u, \qquad 0 \leq u \leq 1.
$$
Writing these parametric equations in the usual notation, we have
$$
x = 0, \qquad y= t, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 1.
$$
These are parametric equations of a line segment. Moreover, the endpoints of $S_1$ are mapped to the $xy$-plane as follows:
$$
\begin{array}{r}\displaystyle \mathbf{T} : ( 0 , 0 ) \to  ( 0 \cdot  ( {0}^{2} + 1 ) , 0 ) = ( 0 , 0 ) \\ \displaystyle \mathbf{T} : ( 1 , 0 ) \to  ( 0 \cdot  ( {1}^{2} + 1 ) , 1 ) = ( 0 , 1 )\end{array}
$$
Therefore, the image of $S_1$ is a line segment traversed from the point $(0,0)$ to $(0,1).$

![](images/13/132642571953ddbfc95c3f0c399cd3c612a2ba2a84a224939b6f40e7d22a074f.png)

- Consider the image of the side $S_2.$ Here, we have $u=1$ and $0 \leq v \leq 1.$ Substituting $u=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain
$$
\begin{array}{rlr}\displaystyle ( x , y ) & \displaystyle  = \mathbf{T} ( u , v ) & \displaystyle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( v ( {u}^{2} + 1 ) , \hspace{0.167em} u ) & \displaystyle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( v ( {1}^{2} + 1 ) , \hspace{0.167em} 1 ) & \displaystyle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( 2 v , \hspace{0.167em} 1 ) , & \displaystyle 0 \le  v \le  1.\end{array}
$$
This horizontal line segment is traversed from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(2,1)$ in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/13/131644a2410e5127a69388f1bd1fced1e28698e7634b137fcd47f8b3f26121a3.png)

- Consider the image of the side $S_3.$ Here, we have $v=1$ and $1 \geq u \geq 0$ (we write the inequality for $u$ in this way to show that $S_3$ is traversed *from* the point where $u=1$ *to* the point where $u=0$).

Substituting $v=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain
$$
\begin{array}{rlr}\displaystyle ( x , y ) & \displaystyle  = \mathbf{T} ( u , v ) & \displaystyle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( v ( {u}^{2} + 1 ) , \hspace{0.167em} u ) & \displaystyle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( 1 ( {u}^{2} + 1 ) , \hspace{0.167em} u ) & \displaystyle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( {u}^{2} + 1 , \hspace{0.167em} u ) , & \displaystyle 1 \ge  u \ge  0.\end{array}
$$
So, the image of $S_3$ can be parametrized by
$$
x = u^2+1, \qquad y= u, \qquad 1 \geq u \geq 0.
$$
Writing these in the usual notation, we have
$$
x = t^2+1, \qquad y= t, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 1.
$$
These are parametric equations of a parabolic arc. Notice that if we eliminate $t$ from the equation, we get
$$
y^2 = x-1
$$
which is a right-opening parabola whose vertex is at $(1,0).$ Moreover, the endpoints of $S_3$ are mapped to the $xy$-plane as follows:
$$
\begin{array}{r}\displaystyle \mathbf{T} : ( 1 , 1 ) \to  ( 1 \cdot  ( {1}^{2} + 1 ) , 1 ) = ( 2 , 1 ) \\ \displaystyle \mathbf{T} : ( 0 , 1 ) \to  ( 1 \cdot  ( {0}^{2} + 1 ) , 0 ) = ( 1 , 0 )\end{array}
$$
Therefore, the image of $S_3$ is an arc of a right-opening parabola, traversed from the point $(2,1)$ to $(1,0).$

![](images/bb/bb73b7c44c9fec45c3c3a632eed03db6f07db3ebbaff9e8e3941d22e78f478db.png)

- Consider the image of the side $S_4.$ Here, we have $u=0$ and $1 \geq v \geq 0.$ Substituting $u=0$ into our transformation equations, we obtain
$$
\begin{array}{rlr}\displaystyle ( x , y ) & \displaystyle  = \mathbf{T} ( u , v ) & \displaystyle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( v ( {u}^{2} + 1 ) , \hspace{0.167em} u ) & \displaystyle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( v ( {0}^{2} + 1 ) , \hspace{0.167em} 0 ) & \displaystyle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( v , \hspace{0.167em} 0 ) , & \displaystyle 1 \ge  v \ge  0.\end{array}
$$ 
This is a horizontal line segment traversed from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane.

![](images/7c/7c72a5f4341ab24df69d1375588abd655abbe8fec77ecd41e52501b602b7e3fb.png)

      

And that's it! We have successfully computed the image of $\Delta$ in the $xy$-plane. 

It's highly recommended that you redo this calculation yourself. Make sure you can construct the image of $\Delta,$ including its orientation (note that the image of $\Delta$ is traversed *clockwise*).

The conditional probability mass function $f_{X|Y}(x|y)$ is defined as

$$
f_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) = P(X = x \,|\, Y=y).
$$

Therefore, we're required to compute the following set of conditional probabilities:

$$
f_{X|Y}(x \,|\, 1) = P(X = x \,|\, Y=1)
$$

By the multiplication law for conditional probability, we have

$$
P(X = x \,|\, Y=1) = \dfrac{P(X = x, Y=1)}{P(Y=1)} = \dfrac{f(x,1)}{f_Y(1)}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and $f_Y(y)$ is the marginal distribution of $Y.$

Recall that the marginal distributions for $X$ and $Y$ correspond to the row and column totals, respectively. So, let's compute these:

| $X=2$ | $0.3$ | $0.1$ | $0$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=4$ | $0.1$ | $0$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ |
| $f_Y(y)$ | $0.5$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ | $1$ |

Therefore, for $x\in \{0,2,4\},$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle P ( X = 0 \hspace{0.167em} | \hspace{0.167em} Y = 1 ) & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{f ( 0 , 1 )}{ {f}_{Y} ( 1 )}} = {\displaystyle \frac{0.1}{0.5}} = {\displaystyle \frac{1}{5}} \\ \displaystyle P ( X = 2 \hspace{0.167em} | \hspace{0.167em} Y = 1 ) & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{f ( 2 , 1 )}{ {f}_{Y} ( 1 )}} = {\displaystyle \frac{0.3}{0.5}} = {\displaystyle \frac{3}{5}} \\ \displaystyle P ( X = 4 \hspace{0.167em} | \hspace{0.167em} Y = 1 ) & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{f ( 4 , 1 )}{ {f}_{Y} ( 1 )}} = {\displaystyle \frac{0.1}{0.5}} = {\displaystyle \frac{1}{5}}\end{array}
$$

Given the supports of $X$ and $Y,$ the joint support $S$ is a subset of

$$
{S}_{X} \times  {S}_{Y} = \{  2 , 4 , 6 , 8 \}  \times  \{  1 , 3 , 5 \}  .
$$

![](images/91/91a0796929c7d023dd3a7110458ec2b9b3c365b8ba433c001707155c65cf4e28.png)

A=PDP^T,

A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is negative-definite if $Q(\mathbf{x}) \lt 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & ={2}^{2}-3\cdot {7}^{2}+5\cdot 2\cdot 7 \\  & =4-147+70 \\  & =-73<0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 7\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 14\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =110>0.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}T(x) & ={7}^{2}+8\cdot 2\cdot 7 \\  & =49+112 \\  & =161>0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{f}_{Y} ( y ) = \left\{  \begin{array}{cc}{f}_{X} ( {u}^{- 1} ( y ) ) \cdot  ∣ ( {u}^{- 1} {)}^{\prime } ( y ) ∣ , & y \text{ is between } u ( a ) \text{ and } u ( b ) \\ 0 , & \text{otherwise} .\end{array} \right. 
$$

The transformation 
$$
u(x) = \dfrac{1-x}{4}
$$
is strictly monotonically *decreasing*, so the change-of-variables method can be used.

First, we find $u^{-1}(y)$. Since

$$
y = \frac{1 - x}{4} ,
$$

we solve for $x$:

$$
\begin{array}{cc}4 y &  = 1 - x \\ x &  = 1 - 4 y .\end{array}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{u}^{- 1} ( y ) = 1 - 4 y .
$$

Then, we find $(u^{-1})'(y){:}$
$$
(u^{-1})'(y) = -4
$$

According to the change-of-variables method, for nonzero $f_Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{array}{cc}{f}_{Y} ( y ) &  = {f}_{X} ( {u}^{- 1} ( y ) ) \cdot  ∣ ( {u}^{- 1} {)}^{\prime } ( y ) ∣ \\  &  = {f}_{X} ( 1 - 4 y ) \cdot  | - 4 | \\  &  = \frac{1}{156} {( 1 - 4 y )}^{3} \cdot  4 \\  &  = \frac{1}{39} {( 1 - 4 y )}^{3} .\end{array}
$$

Finally, since $f_X$ is nonzero on $1 < x < 5,$ the bounds are $a=1$ and $b=5,$ we have
$$
u(1) = 0, \quad u(5) = -1.
$$

Therefore, the probability density function of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y} ( y ) = \left\{  \begin{array}{cc}\frac{1}{39} ( 1 - 4 y {)}^{3} , & - 1 < y < 0 , \\ 0 , & \text{otherwise} .\end{array} \right. 
$$

Notice that we are given a $3 \times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda=-1$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda=3$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1 \times 1$ Jordan block $J_1(3)$ corresponding to $\lambda=3.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda=-1{:}$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2 \times 2$ Jordan block $J_2(-1).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ form the following chain:

$$
\mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A+I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A+I} \mathbf{0}
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1 \times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely $J_1(-1) {\:\oplus\:} J_1(-1).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda=-1.$

Computing $A+I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 7 & 8 \\ -4 & -8 & -9\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 8 & 8 \\ -4 & -8 & -8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 8 & 8 \\ -4 & -8 & -8\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & -8 & -8\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A+I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1,$ say, $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ form the following chains: 

$$
\mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A+I} \mathbf{0} \[5pt]
\mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A+I} \mathbf{0}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

![](images/c5/c59f5929bdbe3b35e42dc30266ac9ca947c3536e1c019b708a2d48170ea8222b.png)

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PDP^T,
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a real matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

The procedure for finding an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3 \times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ is similar to diagonalizing a regular (diagonalizable) $3\times 3$ matrix:

- **Step 1**: Find the eigenvalues of $A.$

- **Step 2**: Find a basis of  $\mathbb{R}^3$ consisting of *unit orthogonal* eigenvectors of $A.$

- **Step 3**: Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

As an example, consider the matrix 
$$
A={\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}- 2 & - 5 & 1 \\ - 5 & - 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & - 8\end{array} \right]}.
$$

This matrix is symmetric. So let's apply our diagonalization algorithm.

- **Step 1.**  We find the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving $\det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ This gives

$$
\lambda_1=3, \qquad \lambda_2=-6, \qquad \lambda_3=-9.
$$

- **Step 2.** We need to find an eigenvector basis of $\mathbb R^3.$ Seeking a nonzero solution of $|A-\lambda_i I| = 0$ for $i=1,2,3,$ we get the corresponding eigenvectors
$$
\mathbf{v}_1 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}, \qquad
\mathbf{v}_2 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}, \qquad
\mathbf{v}_3 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ - 1 \\ 2\end{array} \right]}.
$$
Notice that the eigenvectors are mutually orthogonal. 
Now, an orthogonal diagonalization requires each eigenvector to be normalized. So, dividing each eigenvector by its norm, we obtain the following unit orthogonal eigenvectors:
$$
\mathbf{u}_1

= {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}} \\ 0\end{array} \right]}, \qquad
\mathbf{u}_2

= {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}}\end{array} \right]}, \qquad
\mathbf{u}_3

= {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}} \\ - {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

- **Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ as follows:
$$
D = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{\color{blue}3} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {\color{red}- 6} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {\color{purple}- 9}\end{array} \right]},\qquad
P = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{\color{blue}- {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}} & {\color{red}{\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}}} & {\color{purple}- {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}}} \\ {\color{blue}{\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}} & {\color{red}{\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}}} & {\color{purple}- {\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}}} \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}{\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}}} & {\color{purple}{\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}}}\end{array} \right]}
$$

**Watch out!** In this example, we automatically get orthogonal eigenvectors because $A$ has three *distinct* eigenvalues. However, in the case of repeated eigenvalues, the corresponding eigenvectors might not be orthogonal.

$$

$$

Given a bilinear form $B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ such that 

$$
B:\Bbb R^n \times \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R
$$

and the corresponding $n \times n$ matrix is *symmetric*, we can define the so-called **quadratic form** by substituting $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}$ as follows:

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})= B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}).
$$

 

Notice that the new expression depends only on $\mathbf{x}.$ So, a quadratic form is a function 

$$
Q:\Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R.
$$

In matrix notation, a quadratic form  can be given as 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x},
$$

  

where $A$ is a symmetric matrix. It's called the **matrix of the quadratic form**. 

**Watch out!** By definition, the matrix of a quadratic form must be *symmetric*.

For example, given the bilinear form 

![](images/99/996c4aa136dd7cda56787a2edb0f9481ed3d9356248a27afcde050ca613b6b9c.svg) 

the corresponding quadratic form is then
$Q( \mathbf{x})=B( \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}).$
Explicitly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({x}_{1},{x}_{2}) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

**Note**: In a quadratic form, all terms must be of degree two (considered as polynomials in the variables $x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n$). That's the reason we call it *quadratic*.

In certain applications involving quadratic forms, an important question is whether a particular quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)$ is *always* positive or *always* negative.

We classify quadratic forms using the following terminology:

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **positive-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form

$$
S(\mathbf{x})=8x_1^2+3x_2^2
$$

is positive-definite since
$8x_1^2+3x_2^2 > 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](images/52/52e43ebb6fa34f40a73358f88aed62846332126c4fe080072c211945f54b412a.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **negative-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) <     0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form 

$$
T(\mathbf{x})=-x_1^2-3x_2^2
$$

is negative-definite since
$-x_1^2-3x_2^2 \lt 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](images/a8/a86f80966c04f960823db91bfc8711eef2bf22a81502e69b5048afc5b4799cb2.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **indefinite** if 

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_1) > 0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ and

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_2) <     0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

For example, the form

$$
R(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+2x_2^2-6x_1x_2
$$

is indefinite. Substituting ![](images/09/094a61c791563994cb520b40179d77546f776bfb9148851e211ec8ed326c279a.svg) we get

$$
\begin{aligned}R({x}_{1}) & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot {0}^{2}-6\cdot 1\cdot 0 \\  & =1+0-0 \\  & =1>0,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting ![](images/f4/f4995691f0b24159baeb3cbb1ee51a9f44c72958c9288809f28f387d17b2810d.svg) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}R({x}_{2}) & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot {1}^{2}-6\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =1+2-6 \\  & =-3<0.\end{aligned}
$$

The **singular value decomposition** (or SVD) of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is a factorization of the form

$$
A=U \Sigma V^T,
$$

where

- $\Sigma$ is an $m \times n$ matrix with the singular values of $A$ (ordered from largest to smallest) on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $m \times m$ matrix, and

- $V$ is an orthogonal $n \times n$ matrix.

The columns of $U$ are called the **left singular vectors** of $A,$ and the columns of $V$ are called the **right singular vectors** of $A.$

For example, the matrix ![](images/46/46b29ceb84e2ed98e48642e67277c9bf63d0552bcd07f813a9ffcaf665ff91b7.svg) has the following singular value decomposition:

![](images/29/298933eb0a789ebe57a296088172f6927d1573770824c0b0cffb393eb9894c70.svg)

The singular value decomposition of a matrix $A$ can be thought of as a type of diagonalization that works for *any* $m\times n$ matrix! It's also one of linear algebra's most useful forms of matrix factorization with applications in statistics, image compression, machine learning, and more.

If $X$ is a continuous random variable and $0 \leq p \leq 1,$ then the $100p$th **percentile** is a number $x_p$ such that

$$
P(X \leq x_p) = p.
$$

- In terms of CDF, the *cumulative distribution function* $F(x)$ of $X,$ the $100p$th percentile $x_p$ is a number on the $x$-axis such that

$$
F(x_p) = p.
$$

- In terms of PDF, the *probability density function* $f(x)$ of $X,$ the $100p$th percentile $x_p$ is a number on the $x$-axis such that the area under the graph of $y=f(x)$ to the left of $x$ is equal to $p \mathbin{:}$

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{x_p} f(x) \, \text{d}x = p.
$$

For example, let's find the $4$th percentile of the random variable $X$ if the probability density function of $X$ is given by

![](images/69/69a9f969e3caaa3cc3d896b5a8b6ed566cff3517743519f0c1088e588c3967e7.svg)

The $4$th percentile corresponds to the decimal $p={\color{red}0.04}$ since $100 \cdot 0.04 = 4.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {x}_{0.04}) & ={\int }_{0}^{{x}_{0.04}}\frac{1}{2}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}|}_{0}^{{x}_{0.04}} \\  & =\frac{{{x}_{0.04}}^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $4$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{{x}_{0.04}}^{2}}{4} & =0.04 \\ {{x}_{0.04}}^{2} & =0.16 \\ {x}_{0.04} & =0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we took the positive root because $0 \leq x_{0.04} \leq 2.$

There are a few special percentiles:

- the $25$th percentile is called the **lower quartile**. This is the number $q_1$ such that

$$
P(X \leq q_1) = 0.25.
$$

- the $50$th percentile is called the **median**. This is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(X \leq m) = 0.5.
$$

- the $75$th percentile is called the **upper quartile**. This is the number $q_3$ such that

$$
P(X \leq q_3) = 0.75.
$$

- the **interquartile range** is the difference between the upper and lower quartiles, that is,

$$
IQR = q_3 - q_1.
$$

Given a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}$ with a symmetric matrix $A$,  we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative,

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive,

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Using the same criteria, we can also classify the symmetric matrix $A$ as positive-definite, positive semi-definite, etc.

For example, consider the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/85/8582c8b840b1e4696b9f83cb2c117d67e3b832e40b1ded716e0dcd23752c6f9c.svg)

Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-5-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & -5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )-1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +24 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)(\lambda +6) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-4,\,-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Since all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative, the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) =  \mathbf{x}^T A \, \mathbf{x}$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is negative-definite.

Let $\Delta_i$ for $i=1,2,\ldots,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ 

According to **Sylvester's criterion**, the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$ is 

- positive-definite if and only if $\Delta_i > 0$ for all $i=1,2,\ldots,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,\ldots,n,$ we have $\Delta_i < 0$ when $i$ is odd, and $\Delta_i > 0$ when $i$ is even.

In particular, if $A$ is negative-definite, then the leading principal minors alternate in sign, with the *first* leading principal minors being negative.

For example, consider the matrix 

$$
A =
{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Let's compute its leading leading principal minors:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\mathrm{\Delta }}_{1} & \displaystyle  = {a}_{11} = 2 > 0 \\ \displaystyle {\mathrm{\Delta }}_{2} & \displaystyle  = \left| \begin{array}{cc}\displaystyle 2 & \displaystyle 1 \\ \displaystyle 1 & \displaystyle 1\end{array} \right| = 1 > 0 \\ \displaystyle {\mathrm{\Delta }}_{3} & \displaystyle  = | A | \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = \left| \begin{array}{ccc}\displaystyle 2 & \displaystyle 1 & \displaystyle 0 \\ \displaystyle 1 & \displaystyle 1 & \displaystyle 0 \\ \displaystyle 0 & \displaystyle 0 & \displaystyle 5\end{array} \right| \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 5 \cdot  \left| \begin{array}{cc}\displaystyle 2 & \displaystyle 1 \\ \displaystyle 1 & \displaystyle 1\end{array} \right| \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 5 > 0\end{array}
$$

All leading principal minors are positive. Therefore, by Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$ is positive-definite.

We can write an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix $A$ in terms of a sum of products of its eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

Specifically, if $\mathbf{u}_i$ denotes an orthonormal eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ for $i=1,\ldots, n$, then

$$
A=\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T.
$$

Expressing a symmetric matrix $A$ in this way is called the **spectral decomposition** of $A.$

To demonstrate, let's find the spectral decomposition of the $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/40/408e7471e4ef788758d423af97f5683186f79192fd8933c350d45bb87f089875.svg)

The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1 = 6$ and $\lambda_2 = -4,$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are

![](images/0c/0c22f7dd97e83c358cb3cef1fcc2db902d908140109334a8cf1c22b35b29c6d2.svg)

The spectral decomposition of $A$ is given by

$$
A =\sum_{i=1}^2 \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1 \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2 \mathbf u_2^T,
$$

where $\mathbf u_1$ and $\mathbf u_2$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2,$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the spectral decomposition of $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3\end{bmatrix}+(-4)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 3\end{bmatrix}+(-4)\cdot \frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\underbrace{6}_{{\lambda }_{1}}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{10} & \frac{3}{10} \\ \frac{3}{10} & \frac{9}{10}\end{bmatrix}}_{{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}}+\underbrace{(-4)}_{{\lambda }_{2}}\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{9}{10} & -\frac{3}{10} \\ -\frac{3}{10} & \frac{1}{10}\end{bmatrix}}_{{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T}}.\end{aligned}

A discrete random variable $X$ follows a **discrete uniform distribution** over a set $S$ if each value in $S$ is equally likely. 

The probability mass function for the discrete uniform distribution on a set $S$ is given by

$$
f(x) = {\left\{  \begin{array}{ll}{\displaystyle \frac{1}{| S |}} , \hspace{1em} & x \in  S , \\ 0 , & \text{otherwise} .\end{array} \right. }
$$

When a random variable $X$ follows a discrete uniform distribution over the set $S=\{ s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n\},$ we denote it as

$$
X \sim U \left\{ s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n\right\}
$$

and we say that $X$ is **uniformly distributed** over $S.$

For example, consider the random variable $T\sim U\{1,2,4\}.$ In this case, $S = \{1,2,4\},$ $|S| = 3,$ and therefore the probability mass function for $T$ is

$$
f(t) = {\left\{  \begin{array}{ll}{\displaystyle \frac{1}{3}} , \hspace{1em} & t \in  \{  1 , 2 , 4 \}  , \\ 0 , & \text{otherwise} .\end{array} \right. }
