Recall that the singular values of a real matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](images/a9/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values.

One use for finding the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace is to find the shortest distance between the vector and the subspace.

Given a vector $\mathbf{x}$ and a subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ the **distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$** is given by 

$$
\Vert \mathbf{x} - \textrm{proj}_{S}\mathbf{x} \Vert
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/d1/d10fd1778529183deb6912cebe9d2b7ad405091fe21a261c464d3d22c6d0860b.png)

Let's find the distance between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where

![](images/83/83f52159171e736c7ee9edbd0593442d2282572db667eca483e5a77d0b73c9f7.svg)

The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In this case, we have 
![](images/9e/9eca38b4b340e44108b073e3f939ce29ae96345b9c1870b9e2cc57a98f9cb077.svg)
Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 9\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\hat{x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the distance formula, the distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\hat{x}) & =‖x-\hat{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\hat{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\hat{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\hat{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0-(-2))^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(4-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+0+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and sample variance $s^2.$ Then, for a given value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} +t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

where $P(T > t_{n-1, \alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ and $T \sim T_{n-1}.$ 

The endpoints of our confidence interval are called **confidence limits** and are given by

$$
\overline{x} \pm t_{n-1, \alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Each part of the formula above has a name:

- $\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean

- $\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the standard error of the mean

- $t_{n-1,\alpha/2}$ is the corresponding $t$-score

- $E = t_{n-1, \alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the margin of error

![](images/10/10cd4a425a9668611335a7e80561944d147faaa9152f91fb9ed87378e8c092eb.svg)

So, our confidence interval can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\overset{―}{x}-[\text{margin of error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{margin of error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-[\text{[math]t[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{[math]t[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-{t}_{n-1,\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, & \,\overset{―}{x}+{t}_{n-1,\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}})\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the expression for the confidence interval is very similar to when the population variance was known. The only difference is that we now use the $t$-scores instead of $z$-scores and the sample standard deviation $s$ instead of the population standard deviation $\sigma.$

Finally, since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably.

$$
f_{Y|X}(y \,|\, 1) = 
{\left\{  \begin{array}{ll}4 {y}^{3} , & \hspace{1em} 0 \le  y \le  1 \\ 0 , & \hspace{1em} \text{otherwise}\end{array} \right. }
$$

$$
\mu_{Y|1}=\dfrac{4}{5}.
$$
What is the conditional variance $\textrm{Var}\big[Y \,|\, X=1\big]?$

The conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\textrm{E}\big[Y^2 \,| \, X=x \big] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y^2 \, f_{Y|X}(y \,|\, x) \: \textrm{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{cc}\text{E} [ {Y}^{2}  |  X = 1 ] &  = {\int }_{- \infty }^{\infty } {y}^{2}  {f}_{Y | X} ( y  |  1 )  \text{d} y \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{1} {y}^{2} \cdot  4 {y}^{3}  \text{d} y \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{1} 4 {y}^{5}  \text{d} y \\  &  = {[ \frac{2 {y}^{6}}{3} ]}_{0}^{1} \\  &  = \frac{2}{3} .\end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle \text{Var} [ Y \hspace{0.167em} | \hspace{0.167em} X = 1 ] & \displaystyle  = \text{E} [ {Y}^{2} \hspace{0.167em} | \hspace{0.167em} X = 1 ] - {\mu }_{Y | 1}^{2} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{2}{3}} - {( {\displaystyle \frac{4}{5}} )}^{2} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{2}{3}} - {\displaystyle \frac{16}{25}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{2}{75}} .\end{array}

Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:

![](images/2c/2c717541104571d6dce45dc88e30c4ff2dd42471d2348fe05b7d91ce395adae4.svg)

In other words,

$$
X_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).
$$

Let's assume the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5\%$ of the population size. Under this condition, we've seen that $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n$ can be considered to be (approximately) independent and identically distributed, which means that

$$
X = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p),
$$

where $B(n,p)$ denotes a binomial distribution, and

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).
$$

Remember that $X$ represents the number of sample members with the characteristic.

Now, let's assume that $np > 5$ and $n(1-p) > 5$ so we can apply the normal approximation of the binomial distribution (i.e., the central limit theorem). Then,

$$
X  \approx N\big(np,np(1-p)\big).
$$

Furthermore, we've also seen that we can construct an estimator $\widehat{\,p}$ as

$$
\widehat{\,p} =  \dfrac{X}{n}
$$

where

$$
\textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

Since $X$ is approximately normally distributed, $\widehat{\,p}$ is also normally distributed. Therefore, the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ is given by 

$$
\widehat{\,p}\approx N\bigg(p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\bigg).
$$

Finally, since we usually don't know $p,$ we can use a particular estimate to approximate $\textrm{E}[{\widehat{\,p}}]$ and $\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}].$

**Watch out!** In this lesson, $N$ denotes the size of a population, while $N(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes the normal distribution.

X = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p),
$$

where $B(n,p)$ denotes a binomial distribution, and

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).
$$

Remember that $X$ represents the number of sample members with the characteristic.

Now, let's assume that $np > 5$ and $n(1-p) > 5$ so we can apply the normal approximation of the binomial distribution (i.e., the central limit theorem). Then,

$$
X  \approx N\big(np,np(1-p)\big).
$$

Furthermore, we've also seen that we can construct an estimator $\widehat{\,p}$ as

$$
\widehat{\,p} =  \dfrac{X}{n}
$$

where

$$
\textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

Since $X$ is approximately normally distributed, $\widehat{\,p}$ is also normally distributed. Therefore, the sampling distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ is given by 

$$
\widehat{\,p}\approx N\bigg(p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\bigg).
$$

Finally, since we usually don't know $p,$ we can use a particular estimate to approximate $\textrm{E}[{\widehat{\,p}}]$ and $\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}].$

**Watch out!** In this lesson, $N$ denotes the size of a population, while $N(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes the normal distribution.

Recall that the **probability density function** (or **pdf**) of a continuous random variable $X$ defined over a set $S$ is a function $f(x)$ that satisfies the following conditions:

- $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$ in $S$

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

It is common for the set $S$ of a continuous random variable $X$ to be an infinite interval. Therefore, we often need to evaluate improper integrals when determining whether a function is a valid pdf and to compute probabilities associated with such a random variable.

For example, let's consider the following function:

![](images/38/38ea105f5dd0cea7784bf73f814e7161b90cfd224eb099084cc33b6539d95fdd.svg)

Is $f(x)$ a valid probability density function? Let's start by sketching its graph:

![](images/35/3559a998491a004c159683aaf0946bb4fdf87f4afe873fdc93235e840b4b0ac8.png)

Clearly, $f(x)\geq 0$ for all $x,$ so this function satisfies the first condition.

To check that $f(x)$ satisfies the second condition, we need to compute the following integral:

$$
\int_S f(x)\,\textrm d x = \int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,\textrm d x
$$

Calculating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & ={[-{e}^{-x}]}_{0}^{\infty } \\  & =[-{e}^{-\infty }]-[-{e}^{0}] \\  & =0-(-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $f(x)$ satisfies both conditions, we conclude that $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

The $n$th roots of unity have other interesting properties, which we list below, along with a proof of each result.

When proving the results, assume that $z$ and $w$ are $n$th roots of unity, and therefore $z^n = w^n=1.$

- *A product of two $n$th roots of unity is an $n$th root of unity.*

To prove this, note that
$$
\big(zw\big)^n= z^n\cdot w^n = 1 \cdot 1 = 1,
$$
which means that $zw$ is also an $n$th root of unity.

- *The reciprocal of an $n$th root of unity is an $n$th root of unity.*

To prove this, note that
$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{z}\right)^n= \dfrac{1}{z^n} = \dfrac 1 1 = 1,
$$
which means that $\dfrac 1 z$ is an $n$th root of unity too.

- *The quotient of two $n$th roots of unity is an $n$th root of unity.*

To prove this, note that
$$
\left(\dfrac{z}{w}\right)^n= \dfrac{z^n}{w^n} = \dfrac 1 1 = 1,
$$
which means that $\dfrac z w$ is an $n$th root of unity.

- *Any integer power of an $n$th root of unity is an $n$th root of unity.*

To prove this, note that
$$
\big(z^k\big)^n= \big(z^n\big)^k = 1^k = 1,
$$
which means that $z^k$ is an $n$th root of unity.

$$
M_x = \iint\limits_D y \, \lambda(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.

![](images/06/067543543031a1d8cb4ceb9a7901ad7db77629243adc6658d4a9eab3e98fe09f.png)

$$

$$

and $\lambda(x,y) =  2x.$

$$
\begin{array}{cc}{M}_{x} &  = \underset{D}{\iint } y \cdot  2 x  \text{d} A \\  &  = \underset{D}{\iint } 2 x y  \text{d} A \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{1} {\int }_{0}^{1 - {x}^{2}} 2 x y  \text{d} y  \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{1} 2 x [ {\int }_{0}^{1 - {x}^{2}} y  \text{d} y ]  \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{1} 2 x \cdot  {[ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} ]}_{y = 0}^{y = 1 - {x}^{2}}  \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{1} x {( 1 - {x}^{2} )}^{2}  \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{1} x - 2 {x}^{3} + {x}^{5}  \text{d} x \\  &  = {[ \frac{1}{2} {x}^{2} - \frac{1}{2} {x}^{4} + \frac{1}{6} {x}^{6} ]}_{x = 0}^{x = 1} \\  &  = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{6} \\  &  = \frac{1}{6} .\end{array}
$$

Suppose we wish to find the points of intersection of the elliptic paraboloid 
$z=x^2+y^2$
and the line with the equation
$x = -y = -z+1.$
The line, paraboloid, and their points of intersection are shown below.

![](images/51/5159ac99a1bc9f73c01df3c2cc2e6fb2093a3d68e00731609d7b62a6fa55149d.png)

 

The trick is to express the equation of the line in parametric form, substitute the parametric equations into the equation of the surface, and solve for the parameter.

So, first, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

![](images/01/01357a5c6b72d7c976765aeed04db8afa3e3a80e13095d9be1ea2f2594ae5bf5.svg)

where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Our intersection points must belong to the line and the surface simultaneously. So, substituting the expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ from the parametric equation of the line into the equation of the paraboloid, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ (-t+1) & =(t)^{2}+(-t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying this equation, we get

$$
2t^2+t - 1=0.
$$

The solutions to this equation are
$t=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $t=-1.$ 

Substituting these values back into the parametric equations of the line

- For $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \\ y=-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{1}{2} \\ z=-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+1=\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}).$

- For $t=-1$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=(-1)=-1 \\ y=-(-1)=1 \\ z=-(-1)+1=2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(-1,1,2).$

Therefore, the points of intersection are $(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2})$ and $(-1,1,2).$

It's possible to derive Taylor polynomials for functions of more than two variables. However, increasing the number of variables significantly increases the number of terms in the Taylor polynomial. 

Ideally, we'd like a compact expression for the quadratic Taylor polynomial that works for all twice-differentiable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.$ This can be achieved using matrix notation. 

To see how, let's consider the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f(x,y)$ about $(a,b){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overbrace{f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} \\  & \,\,+\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2})}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote ![](images/6f/6fe1832d2f4ae2b36446386e5d0ec7c41f898f4e575af9238695c37f7c427250.svg) and ![](images/49/496eacb98651e3fab4c0d0a7b44ab283fadad1c07243da485aeb0c4a059d5712.svg) then the total derivative of $f(x,y)=f(\mathbf{x})$ at $(a,b)=\mathbf{a}$ is given by

![](images/d6/d696700e295d9f43111ac53602b936a991b7766af654cedaa5afdae21b088a59.svg)

With that in mind, we can rewrite the linear part of the approximation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Linear approximation} & =f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b) \\  & =f(a)+[\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-a \\ y-b\end{aligned}] \\  & =f(a)+[\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]) \\  & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is just our usual linear approximation of a function $f.$

The second derivative of $f$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is given by

![](images/de/de2a75a6681e1e393b21b60de9d7aeee748a8e6d04010ab713b40f0f41f239cf.svg)

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Quadratic part} & =\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}x-a & y-b\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-a \\ y-b\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}([\begin{aligned}x & y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a & b\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈\overbrace{f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this formula is more compact and has clear similarity with the corresponding formula for functions with one variable:

$$
f(x) \approx  \overbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{Quadratic part}}
$$

![](images/df/dfa82e503eeaa38943edddc7d6982cf4893c73fd2f6d075dd390f51cd0450091.svg)

By restricting $\mathbf x$ to a line through $\mathbf{a},$ we can consider $f$ as a function of one variable. Then, we'll use the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a single-variable function to derive the formula.

Let $\mathbf{x}_0$ be a constant vector in $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Then, the line through $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}_0$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a}), \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty),
$$

where $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}(1) = \mathbf{x}_0.$

Now, we define a function $F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by restricting the domain of $f$ to this line:

$$
F(t)
= f(\mathbf{x}(t))
%= f(\mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a}))
$$

The second-degree Taylor polynomial of this single-variable function about $t=0$ is given by

$$
F(t) \approx F(0) + F'(0)t + \dfrac12F''(0)t^2.
$$

We can find the first derivative of $F$ using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a+t({x}_{0}-a)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf{x}}$ is a row vector and $(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a})$ is a column vector, this is a scalar quantity and, hence, equal to its transpose:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a) \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a))}^{T} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}F}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}) \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\left(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}f}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}({x}_{0}-a)\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & ≈F(0)+{F}^{′}(0)t+\frac{1}{2}{F}^{″}(0){t}^{2} \\  & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)t+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a){t}^{2}\end{aligned}

$$

Let’s derive a general rule for the gradient of a linear function.

Suppose $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ and the scalar function $f$ is given by

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b}^T \mathbf{x},
$$

where $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a fixed vector. 

We wish to find an expression for the gradient of $f.$

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f = \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{b}^T \mathbf{x})
$$

To do this, let's write our vectors $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf x$ explicitly:

![](images/8a/8a824abda10928a55f4efd94f7c0e4bff0dabf13fc44b789ed53e829971c3471.svg)

Then, $\mathbf b^T \mathbf x$ is the scalar function

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}^{T}x & =\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & … & {b}_{n}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
\mathbf b^T \mathbf x
=b_1x_1+ b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_nx_n.
$$

The partial derivative of $\mathbf b^T \mathbf x$ with respect to $x_i$ is $b_i,$ since all the other terms will vanish. 

$$
\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left(\mathbf b^T\mathbf x\right) = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left(b_1x_1+ b_2x_2 + \cdots + b_i x_i + \cdots + b_nx_n\right) = b_i
$$

Since this is true for all $1\leq i\leq n,$ we have

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf x} \left(\mathbf b^T \mathbf x\right) = \mathbf b
$$

as required.

This is the multivariable analog of the familiar rule from single-variable calculus:

$$
\frac{\textrm d}{\textrm dx}(a x) = a
$$

Recall that the gradient of a function 

$$

$$

tells us how the function changes with respect to each of its input variables. It collects all the partial derivatives into a single vector:

![](images/fe/fe9b4aa3c2e46dceeb10f63c021232f88ff1d3bd71f40fbd464b2ddb1cabef4a.svg)

We only need the derivatives with respect to the variables we care about.

This idea leads us to the concept of the **subset gradient**, which captures how a function changes with respect to only a chosen group of variables while treating the others as constant.

Just as we can compute gradients with respect to a subset of variables, we can also take second derivatives while focusing on just the variables that matter for our problem. 

When we write $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}(\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} f)$, we are computing all second-order partial derivatives of the function $f$ with respect to the variables in $\mathbf{w}.$ The result is a square matrix where each entry describes how one component of the gradient changes when we vary one of the selected variables. This matrix is the **Hessian with respect to** $\mathbf{w}.$

To make this concrete, suppose we have a function $f(x, y, z)$ that depends on three variables. If we only care about second derivatives with respect to $x$ and $y$, we write $\nabla_{x,y}(\nabla_{x,y} f).$

This gives us a $2 \times 2$ matrix that contains the following second-order partial derivatives

![](images/89/895686eb22d040a761ca4edfb8d5b65ca23c23cb06aadc63ce05be06a66d193c.svg)

Even though $f$ depends on three variables, this matrix isolates the second-derivative behavior of $f$ in just the $x$ and $y$ directions. This allows us to analyze or optimize over part of the input space without involving every variable.

Let’s go through a concrete example.  

Consider the function

$$
f(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{w}) = w_1^2 x_2^2 - w_2 x_1,
$$

and suppose we want to compute the Hessian with respect to $\mathbf{w} = [w_1, \, w_2]^T.$

First, we compute the gradient:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{w}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{w}_{1}}({w}_{1}^{2}{x}_{2}^{2}-{w}_{2}{x}_{1})=2{w}_{1}{x}_{2}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂{w}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{w}_{2}}({w}_{1}^{2}{x}_{2}^{2}-{w}_{2}{x}_{1})=-{x}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

![](images/52/52bd7d2b21c9d884017376168f82fe4612157f0d92802d78e98d72b90f6f1658.svg)

This is the Hessian with respect to the parameter vector $\mathbf{w}.$ It tells us how the gradient of the function (with respect to parameters) changes when we vary each parameter and reveals the local shape of the function near any given point.

In this lesson, we’ll continue exploring the *total derivative* of a vector-valued function, which generalizes the derivative to functions with multiple inputs and outputs.

Suppose a transformation $\boldsymbol{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined by 

$$
𝒇:{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ \vdots  \\ {x}_{n}\end{array} \right]}
\longrightarrow
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{f}_{1} ( {x}_{1} , {x}_{2} , \ldots  , {x}_{n} ) \\ {f}_{2} ( {x}_{1} , {x}_{2} , \ldots  , {x}_{n} ) \\ \vdots  \\ {f}_{m} ( {x}_{1} , {x}_{2} , \ldots  , {x}_{n} )\end{array} \right]},
$$ 

where $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_m$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables.

If $\boldsymbol f$ is differentiable at $\mathbf{x},$ then the **total derivative** of $\boldsymbol f$ at $\mathbf{x},$ denoted $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}),$ is given by the $m \times n$ matrix

$$
𝒇'(\mathbf x) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}𝒇}{\textrm{d}\mathbf x} 
=
{\left[ \begin{array}{cccc}{\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{1}}{\partial  {x}_{1}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{1}}{\partial  {x}_{2}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{1}}{\partial  {x}_{n}}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{2}}{\partial  {x}_{1}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{2}}{\partial  {x}_{2}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{2}}{\partial  {x}_{n}}} \\ \vdots  & \vdots  & \vdots  & \vdots  \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{m}}{\partial  {x}_{1}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{m}}{\partial  {x}_{2}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  {f}_{m}}{\partial  {x}_{n}}}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

This is sometimes called the **Jacobian matrix** of $\boldsymbol{f}$ at $\mathbf{x}$. Each row corresponds to the derivative of one component function $f_i$, and each column corresponds to the rate of change of all the components of $\boldsymbol f$ with respect to one input variable $x_j$. This is sometimes called the **numerator layout** for derivatives because each row corresponds to each function component, which appears in the numerator positions of the partial derivatives.

Notice that if $f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a scalar-valued function, then the total derivative is a row vector given by
  $$
f'(\mathbf{x}) = 
  {\left[ \begin{array}{cccc}{\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {x}_{1}}} & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {x}_{2}}} & \cdots  & {\displaystyle \frac{\partial  f}{\partial  {x}_{n}}}\end{array} \right]} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n}.
$$

On the other hand, if $\boldsymbol{f}: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is a vector-valued function of a single variable, then the total derivative is a column vector
  $$
𝒇'(x) =
  {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\displaystyle \frac{\mathrm{d} {f}_{1}}{\mathrm{d} x}} \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\mathrm{d} {f}_{2}}{\mathrm{d} x}} \\ \vdots  \\ {\displaystyle \frac{\mathrm{d} {f}_{m}}{\mathrm{d} x}}\end{array} \right]} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times 1}.
$$

Now let’s get some practice by working through a few examples of total derivatives.

The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ is the Jacobian of $\boldsymbol f$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as 

$$
J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\mathbf{x}_n) = -\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-{y}^{2}+5) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3} & -2y \\ 2x & -3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}4 {x}^{3} & - 2 y \\ 2 x & - 3 {y}^{2}\end{array} \right]}_{\mathbf{x}_n}
(\mathbf{x}_{n+1} -  \mathbf{x}_n)
=
-{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{x}^{4} - {y}^{2} + 5 \\ {x}^{2} - {y}^{3} + 1\end{array} \right]}_{\mathbf{x}_n}.
$$

$$
v_1 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 0.71 \\ - 0.71\end{array} \right]},
$$

which points in the direction of maximum variance. To obtain a one-dimensional representation of the data, we project each row of $X$ onto this direction by computing

$$
Xv_1 = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0.4 & 0.6 \\ - 1.5 & - 1.5 \\ 0.4 & 0.3 \\ 0.7 & 0.6\end{array} \right]} {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 0.71 \\ - 0.71\end{array} \right]} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 0.71 \\ 2.13 \\ - 0.50 \\ - 0.92\end{array} \right]}.
$$

![](images/73/73f9917800e09dcaba4d3eb544320d441621b0fb7bd3fd7f31b109501b2f3aad.svg)

For example, let's construct the adjacent matrix for the relation

|  | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ |  |  |  |
| $2$ |  |  |  |
| $3$ |  |  |  |

To fill in the matrix, we run over the ordered pairs in our relation:

- Since $(1,2)$ belongs to the relation, we write $1$ in the intersection of the $1$st row and $2$nd column.

- Since $(1,3)$ belongs to the relation, we write $1$ in the intersection of the $1$st row and $3$rd column.

- Since $(2,1)$ belongs to the relation, we write $1$ in the intersection of the $2$nd row and $1$st column.

- Since $(3,2)$ belongs to the relation, we write $1$ in the intersection of the $3$rd row and $2$nd column.

|  | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |

The Wronskian is a quick way to check whether two solutions of a homogeneous ODE are linearly independent.

In this lesson, we learn an identity, which tells us how the Wronskian changes with $x$ for an equation of the form 

$$
y''+P(x)y'+Q(x)y=0.
$$

Suppose $y_1$ and $y_2$ are solutions of the second-order linear homogeneous ODE above on some interval $I.$ Let $W(x)$ be their Wronskian:
![](images/bf/bf982a342681e4142c476f52c77cb95836bc024d75a0c62961fc5f0d6d71320b.svg)

Then, **Abel's identity** states that the Wronskian satisfies the first-order linear differential equation

$$
W'(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

Solving this equation via separation of variables gives the general form for $W(x){:}$

$$
W(x) = C e^{-\int P(x) \, \text{d}x}
$$

This allows us to determine the behavior of the Wronskian without knowing the solutions $y_1$ and $y_2.$

For example, consider the second-order homogeneous differential equation 

$$
y''+3xy'+e^x y=0
$$

with solutions $y_1$ and $y_2,$ and the corresponding Wronskian $W(x).$ Let's determine the differential equation that $W(x)$ must satisfy.

In our equation, the coefficient of $y'$ is 

$$
P(x)=3x.
$$

Substituting this into Abel's identity gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′}(x) & =-3xW(x).\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** If the equation is not already in standard form, we should rewrite it before applying Abel’s identity.

In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
![](images/6f/6f6a92e2b8fb89f833268a5526876cb3af5215db0193a2aaaad8aac5790752ea.svg)
when the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has at least one *zero eigenvalue*.

A zero eigenvalue is special because $e^{0\cdot t}=1,$ so the corresponding component of a solution has *no exponential growth or decay*. Geometrically, this often creates a **line of equilibrium points** (infinitely many fixed points), instead of a single equilibrium at the origin.

Indeed, equilibrium points satisfy $\mathbf{x}'=\mathbf{0},$ so for $\mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x}$ we solve

$$
A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

That is, equilibrium points form the *null space* of $A.$

- If $\det(A) \neq 0,$ then the null space is $\{\mathbf{0}\}$ and the only equilibrium is the origin.

- If $\det(A)=0,$ then the null space contains infinitely many points (typically a line through the origin in $2\times2$ cases).

A zero eigenvalue guarantees $\det(A)=0$, so in that case the null space is nontrivial.

Let's see a concrete example.

To set the stage, let's first recall how to calculate a percentage increase in a retail situation.

Recall that *increasing* the price of the meal by $20\%$ means that we must apply a new percentage of

$$
100\% + 20\% = 120\%.
$$

Thus, the new price is $120\%$ of the old price.

Expressing $120\%$ as a decimal, we have

$$
120\% = \dfrac{120}{100} = 1.2.
$$

Now, we multiply the original price by $1.2{:}$

$$
\$10 \times 1.2 = \$12
$$

So, the price of the meal after the increase is $\$12.$

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),
$$

For example, consider the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-5x(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Recall that given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

Since we have already seen how to compute the standard fundamental matrix, we will not repeat the calculation here. So, computing the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system, we get

$$

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

**Note:** Recall that for the general solution of the ordinary differential equation $x'(t)=ax(t),$ we have

\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad

\quad
c \in \mathbb{R}.

\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)

Let's find the complementary solution to the following inhomogeneous ODE:
$$
y' + 10y = x - 8
$$

To find the complementary solution $y_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous ODE.
We start by setting the right-hand side equal to zero:
$$
y'_c + 10y_c = 0
$$

Notice that this differential equation is separable since we can write it as
$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y_c}{\textrm{d}x} = -10y_c.
$$

We separate the variables as follows:
$$
\frac{1}{{y}_{c}}  \frac{\text{d} {y}_{c}}{\text{d} x} = - 10
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$
$$
\begin{array}{cc}\int  \frac{1}{{y}_{c}}  \frac{\text{d} {y}_{c}}{\text{d} x}  \text{d} x &  = \int  - 10  \text{d} x \\ \int  \frac{1}{{y}_{c}}  \text{d} {y}_{c} &  = \int  - 10  \text{d} x \\ \ln   | {y}_{c} | &  = - 10 x + C\end{array}
$$

Next, we make $y_c$ the subject by exponentiating both sides:
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle | {y}_{c} | & \displaystyle  = {e}^{- 10 x + C} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {e}^{- 10 x} {e}^{C} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = K {e}^{- 10 x} ,\end{array}
$$
where $K=e^{C}.$

Finally, we can drop the absolute value by allowing the constant to be positive or negative (absorbing the sign into the constant).
Therefore, the complementary solution is
$$
y_c(x)=Ae^{-10x},
$$
where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

after:
A standard vibrating system under an external force $f(t)$ looks like
$$
y''+\omega^2y=f(t),
$$
where $\omega$ is the system's natural **internal frequency**.

The complementary solution $y_c$ describes the system's internal oscillation when there is no external force. It can be written as
$$
y_c = A\cos(\omega t) + B\sin(\omega t),
$$
so the motion naturally oscillates at frequency $\omega.$

If the external force $f(t)$ is periodic, then it has its own forcing frequency $\omega_e.$ **Resonance** occurs when the forcing frequency matches the natural frequency:
$$
\omega_e=\omega
$$

Intuitively, resonance happens because the force repeatedly "pushes" the system at exactly the right rhythm each cycle. In the undamped model, these pushes continually add energy to the system at just the right phase, causing the oscillation amplitude to grow without bound.

For example, suppose the position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with periodically forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation
$$
y'' + 36y = -6\cos^2{pt},
$$
where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Let's find the value of the parameter $p$ that causes the oscillator to resonate.

Notice that the complementary solution has frequency $\omega,$ where $\omega^2=36.$ Therefore,
$$
\omega=6.
$$

The external force is
$$
f ( t ) = - 6 {\cos }^{2}  p t = - 3 ( 1 + \cos   2 p t ) ,
$$
which has forcing frequency $\omega_e=2p.$

Resonance occurs when $\omega_e=\omega,$ so
$$
p=\dfrac{\omega}{2} = 3.
$$

$$

$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $xz$-plane is a circle.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type III region:
$$
R = \{  ( x , y , z ) : ( x , z ) \in  D , \text{ } {x}^{2} + {z}^{2} \le  y \le  2 - {x}^{2} - {z}^{2} \}  ,
$$
where $D$ is the interior of the circle ${x}^{2} + {z}^{2} = 1.$

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by
$$
\begin{array}{cc}V &  = \underset{R}{\iiint } \text{d} V \\  &  = \underset{D}{\iint } [ {\int }_{{x}^{2} + {z}^{2}}^{2 - {x}^{2} - {z}^{2}} \text{d} y ] \text{d} A \\  &  = \underset{D}{\iint } ( ( 2 - {x}^{2} - {z}^{2} ) - ( {x}^{2} + {z}^{2} ) ) \text{d} A \\  &  = \underset{D}{\iint } ( 2 - 2 {x}^{2} - 2 {z}^{2} ) \text{d} A .\end{array}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of

- the lower part $z = - \sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}} ,$ and

- the upper part $z = \sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}} ,$

for $- 1 \le  x \le  1.$

$$

$$

$$

- $\overset{\to -}{P C}$ and $\mathbf a$ have opposite directions

A function $f(x)$ is **piecewise smooth** on $x\in[a,b]$ if

- $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous on $[a,b],$ and

- $f'(x)$ exists and is continuous except possibly at finitely many points, where its one-sided limits exist and are finite.

With that in mind, let's examine each function.

- The function $f ( x ) = {x}^{2} + | x |$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in[-2,2].$ We split the interval at $x=0$ into the two open intervals $(-2,0)$ and $(0,2).$ On these intervals,
$$
f ( x ) = \left\{  \begin{array}{cc}{x}^{2} - x , & x < 0 \\ {x}^{2} + x , & x > 0\end{array} \right.   ,
$$
so
$$
{f}^{\prime } ( x ) = \left\{  \begin{array}{cc}2 x - 1 , & x < 0 \\ 2 x + 1 , & x > 0\end{array} \right. 
$$
Here, $f(x)$ and $f'(x)$ are piecewise continuous on each open interval, and they both have finite limits at the endpoints of the subintervals.

- The function $g(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in[-2,2].$ We split the interval at $x=0.$ On each open interval, $(-2,0)$ and $(0,2),$ the function is linear. On these intervals,
$$
g ( x ) = \left\{  \begin{array}{cc}x , & x < 0 \\ x + 2 , & x > 0\end{array} \right.   ,
$$
so
$$
{g}^{\prime } ( x ) = \left\{  \begin{array}{cc}1 , & x < 0 \\ 1 , & x > 0\end{array} \right. 
$$
Here, $g(x)$ and ${g}^{\prime } ( x )$ are piecewise continuous on each open interval, and they both have finite limits at the endpoints of the subintervals.

- The function $\mathrm{ℎ} ( x ) = {x}^{2 / 3}$ is not piecewise smooth on $x\in[-2,2].$ For $x \ne  0 ,$
$$
{\mathrm{ℎ}}^{\prime } ( x ) = \frac{2}{3 {x}^{1 / 3}} .
$$
While this derivative is continuous on the open pieces $(-2,0)$ and $(0,2),$ the limits of the derivative as $x\to 0$ are not finite. In fact, the derivative becomes unbounded near $x=0.$ Thus, the condition for finite limits at the endpoints is not met.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$f$ and $g$ only."

We can still find a position vector by tracing a path from the origin to the point and adding the vectors along that path.

However, if one part of the path points in the opposite direction to a known vector, then we write it as a **negative** multiple of that vector.

For example, consider the picture below. 

![](images/d5/d5366a68ed98e7f614ff998f69098613ea8e12d05bc27274ea66e8ce5a908cb7.png)

We are given that $\mathbf{c} = \lambda  \mathbf{a} + 2 \mathbf{b}$ and we are asked to find $\lambda.$

To find $\lambda,$ we want to match the expression
$$
\mathbf{c} = \lambda  \mathbf{a} + 2 \mathbf{b} .
$$

Let $O$ be the origin, and let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf c$ end at points $A$ and $C,$ as shown in the diagram below.

Since one term in the vector sum is $2 \mathbf{b} ,$ we first draw the vector $2 \mathbf{b}$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

![](images/bc/bc976b12b4610c69953545d95662bf5535ef2a92eb9d9cbd63e087c85f3b98e7.png)

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $2 \mathbf{b} .$ Then

$$
\mathbf{c} = \overset{\to -}{O P} + \overset{\to -}{P C} .
$$

From the construction, we have

$$
\overset{\to -}{O P} = 2 \mathbf{b} .
$$

Also, the vector $\overset{\to -}{P C}$ has length $2 | \mathbf{a} | ,$ but points in the opposite direction to $\mathbf a.$ Therefore,

$$
\overset{\to -}{P C} = - 2 \mathbf{a} .
$$

Substituting these into the expression for $\mathbf{c},$ we get

$$
\begin{array}{cc}\mathbf{c} &  = \overset{\to -}{O P} + \overset{\to -}{P C} \\  &  = 2 \mathbf{b} + ( - 2 \mathbf{a} ) \\  &  = - 2 \mathbf{a} + 2 \mathbf{b} .\end{array}
$$

Consequently,
$$
\mathbf{c} = \lambda  \mathbf{a} + 2 \mathbf{b} = - 2 \mathbf{a} + 2 \mathbf{b} .
$$

Since $\mathbf{a} \nparallel \mathbf{b},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf a,$ we get

$$
\lambda=-2.
$$

Suppose we have two vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf{b},$ and a parallelogram $OAXB_1,$ where $\overset{\to -}{O {B}_{1}} = 2 \overset{\to -}{O B} .$ How can we find the position vector $\mathbf{x} = \overset{\to -}{O X}$ in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf{b}?$

![](images/c7/c78c8895790b28c7dbe60d0dd31a5375fef19ba2d6fa668144859e6fafaf33bb.png)

As before, we trace a path from the origin to the point $X.$ From the diagram, we can write
$$
\mathbf{x} = \overset{\to -}{O {B}_{1}} + \overset{\to -}{{B}_{1} X} .
$$

We know that
$$
\overset{\to -}{O {B}_{1}} = 2 \overset{\to -}{O B} = 2 \mathbf{b} .
$$

Also, since $OAXB_1$ is a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and parallel. So,
$$
\overrightarrow{B_1X}=\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a}.
$$

Substituting these into the expression for $\mathbf x,$ we get
$$
\begin{array}{cc}\mathbf{x} &  = \overset{\to -}{O {B}_{1}} + \overset{\to -}{{B}_{1} X} \\  &  = 2 \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{a} \\  &  = \mathbf{a} + 2 \mathbf{b} .\end{array}
$$

Now we will use the same path-tracing idea in a slightly different way. Instead of only writing a position vector, we will also use vector paths to identify unknown coefficients in linear combinations of known vectors.

So far, we have studied *piecewise continuity*, which allows a function to have finitely many simple discontinuities on an interval.

Sometimes, however, we need a stronger condition: not only should the function behave well on each piece, but its *derivative* should also behave well on each piece.

A function $f(x)$ is **piecewise smooth** on $x\in[a,b]$ if both $f$ and $f'$ are piecewise continuous on $[a,b].$ In other words, $f$ is piecewise smooth on $[a,b]$ if

- $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous on $[a,b],$ and

- $f'(x)$ exists and is continuous except possibly at finitely many points, where its one-sided limits exist and are finite.

In other words, a piecewise-smooth function may have finitely many breakpoints, but between those points the function and its derivative behave well, and the derivative cannot become unbounded.

When a solid is described in words, we first identify its bounding surfaces and then decide how to describe the entire region with inequalities.

A useful strategy is:

- identify the variable that lies between a lower surface and an upper surface,

- determine the projection of the solid onto a coordinate plane,

- write bounds for the projected region,

- use those bounds to set up a triple integral with integrand equal to $1$.

In many volume problems, the solid lies between a bottom surface
$$
z = {z}_{\text{b}} ( x , y )
$$
and a top surface
$$
z = {z}_{\text{t}} ( x , y ) .
$$

In that case, we describe the solid by
$$
R = \{  ( x , y , z ) : ( x , y ) \in  D , \text{ } {z}_{\text{b}} ( x , y ) \le  z \le  {z}_{\text{t}} ( x , y ) \}  ,
$$
where $D$ is the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane.

So, to find the volume, we use
$$
V = {\iiint }_{R} \text{d} V = {\iint }_{D} {\int }_{{z}_{\text{b}} ( x , y )}^{{z}_{\text{t}} ( x , y )} \text{d} z  \text{d} A .
$$

So, the verbal description tells us two things:

- which surface is below and which is above,

- which points $(x,y)$ belong to the base region $D$.

Before integrating, it is always a good idea to check that the upper surface is actually above the lower surface on the entire projected region.

Consider the volume of the solid region enclosed by the $xy$-plane, the plane $z = 4 - x - y ,$ and the planes $x=0,$ $x=2,$ $y=0,$ and $y=1.$

Notice that our solid can be written as a type I region.

First, the phrase **enclosed by the $xy$-plane** tells us that the bottom of the solid is
$$
z=0.
$$

The plane
$$
z = 4 - x - y
$$
is the top of the solid.

Also, the planes
$$
x = 0 ,  x = 2 ,  y = 0 ,  y = 1
$$
describe the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. So the base region is the rectangle
$$
D = \{  ( x , y ) : 0 \le  x \le  2 , \text{ } 0 \le  y \le  1 \}  .
$$

Therefore, for each point $(x,y)$ in this rectangle, the variable $z$ runs from the bottom surface to the top surface:
$$
0 \le  z \le  4 - x - y .
$$

So the volume is
$$
V = {\iiint }_{R} \text{d} V = {\int }_{0}^{2} {\int }_{0}^{1} {\int }_{0}^{4 - x - y} \text{d} z  \text{d} y  \text{d} x .
$$

Now we evaluate:

$$
\begin{array}{cc}V &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} {\int }_{0}^{1} {[ z ]}_{z = 0}^{z = 4 - x - y} \text{d} y  \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} {\int }_{0}^{1} ( 4 - x - y )  \text{d} y  \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} {[ ( 4 - x ) y - \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} ]}_{y = 0}^{y = 1} \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} ( 4 - x - \frac{1}{2} ) \text{d} x \\  &  = {\int }_{0}^{2} ( \frac{7}{2} - x ) \text{d} x \\  &  = {[ \frac{7}{2} x - \frac{{x}^{2}}{2} ]}_{0}^{2} \\  &  = 7 - 2 \\  &  = 5.\end{array}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the solid is $5.$

In problems like this, the planes involving only $x$ and $y$ usually describe the base region in the $xy$-plane, while the $xy$-plane and the surface or plane involving $z$ describe the lower and upper bounds for $z$.

$$

$$

This means that for each point $(x,y)$ in the projection region $D,$ the variable $z$ runs from the lower surface 
$$
z = {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 1
$$
up to the upper surface 
$$
z = 1 - {x}^{2} - {y}^{2} .
$$

$$

$$
V = {\iint }_{D} ( \text{upper surface} - \text{lower surface} )  \text{d} A ,
$$
where $D$ is the projection region in the $xy$-plane.

First, we find where the two surfaces intersect. This gives the boundary of the projection region in the $xy$-plane:
$$
\begin{array}{cc}{x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 1 &  = 1 - {x}^{2} - {y}^{2} \\ 2 {x}^{2} + 2 {y}^{2} &  = 2 \\ {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} &  = 1.\end{array}
$$

So, the projection region $D$ is the disk
$$
{x}^{2} + {y}^{2} \le  1.
$$

The height of the solid is the difference between the upper surface ($z = 1 - {x}^{2} - {y}^{2}$) and the lower surface ($z = {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 1$):
$$
f ( x , y ) = ( 1 - {x}^{2} - {y}^{2} ) - ( {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 1 ) = 2 - 2 {x}^{2} - 2 {y}^{2} .
$$

If we write $D$ using $x$ as the outer variable, then
$$
- 1 \le  x \le  1 ,  - \sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}} \le  y \le  \sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}} .
$$

The volume is given by the iterated integral:
$$
V = {\int }_{- 1}^{1} {\int }_{- \sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}}}^{\sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}}} ( 2 - 2 {x}^{2} - 2 {y}^{2} )  \text{d} y  \text{d} x
$$

To identify the greatest irrational number, we can find the consecutive whole numbers between which each root lies.

- $\sqrt[3]{120}$ lies between $4$ and $5,$ since ${4}^{3} = 64$ and $5^3=125.$

- $\sqrt{18}$ lies between $4$ and $5,$ since ${4}^{2} = 16$ and ${5}^{2} = 25.$

Comparing these bounds, the greatest number must be between $5$ and $6.$ So, it is either $\sqrt{33}$ or $\sqrt{35} .$

When we order irrational roots, we can often compare their whole-number intervals first. A root between $5$ and $6$ is greater than any root between $4$ and $5.$

Suppose we want to identify the greatest number in this list:
$$
\sqrt{28} ,  \sqrt{34} ,  \sqrt[3]{50} ,  \sqrt[3]{115} ,  \sqrt{18} .
$$

We first bracket each root.

- $\sqrt{28}$ lies between $5$ and $6,$ since $25 < 28 < 36.$

- $\sqrt{34}$ lies between $5$ and $6,$ since $25 < 34 < 36.$

- $\sqrt[3]{50}$ lies between $3$ and $4,$ since $27 < 50 < 64.$

- $\sqrt[3]{115}$ lies between $4$ and $5,$ since $64 < 115 < 125.$

- $\sqrt{18}$ lies between $4$ and $5,$ since $16 < 18 < 25.$

The greatest value must be one of the roots between $5$ and $6,$ so it is either $\sqrt{28}$ or $\sqrt{34} .$ Since $34 > 28 ,$ we know $\sqrt{34} > \sqrt{28} .$

Therefore, the greatest number is $\sqrt{34} .$

**Watch out!** We can compare radicands directly only when the roots are the same kind. For example, comparing $\sqrt{34}$ and $\sqrt{28}$ is safe because both are square roots.

$$
\begin{array}{cc}2 \sqrt{x + 6} + 3 - 3 &  = 13 - 3 \\ 2 \sqrt{x + 6} &  = 10\end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{cc}\frac{2 \sqrt{x + 6}}{2} &  = \frac{10}{2} \\ \sqrt{x + 6} &  = 5\end{array}
$$

Now that the radical is isolated, we square both sides to remove the square root:
$$
\begin{array}{cc}{( \sqrt{x + 6} )}^{2} &  = {5}^{2} \\ x + 6 &  = 25\end{array}
$$

To solve for $x,$ we subtract $6$ from both sides:
$$
\begin{array}{cc}x + 6 - 6 &  = 25 - 6 \\ x &  = 19\end{array}
$$

$$

A **permutation** is a function that maps some ordering of numbers to another ordering of numbers.

For example, observe that for three numbers in the order $1,2,3$ there are $6$ different ways to re-order them:

$$

So, there are $6$ different ways, or there are $6$ different functions that map an ordering of $3$ numbers to another ordering of $3$ numbers, which means there are $6$ permutations of the numbers $1,2,3.$

- The permutation $\sigma_1$ maps $1,2,3$ to $1,2,3.$ This permutation is called the **identity permutation** because it keeps the order the same. So, we have

$$
\sigma_1(1) = 1, \quad \sigma_1(2) = 2, \quad \sigma_1(3)=3.
$$

![](images/42/42bde7063227173a99065082bd60c27569833790646109c758d7c72a6fb059a5.png)

- The permutation $\sigma_2$ maps $1,2,3$ to $1,3,2.$ So, we have

$$
\sigma_2(1) = 1, \quad \sigma_2(2) = 3, \quad \sigma_2(3)=2.
$$

![](images/27/27763e91f1630a8afa738989b4ed0ba325e34c3527e7432f862028622cf1e5da.png)

- The permutation $\sigma_3$ maps $1,2,3$ to $2,1,3.$ So, we have

$$
\sigma_3(1) = 2, \quad \sigma_3(2) = 1, \quad \sigma_3(3)=3.
$$

![](images/25/25579fe8cc2decc1c1f86a24c1e9f4e9ce2861a9e39c8f757884f73cd162985b.png)

- The permutation $\sigma_4$ maps $1,2,3$ to $2,3,1.$ So, we have

$$
\sigma_4(1) = 2, \quad \sigma_4(2) = 3, \quad \sigma_4(3)=1.
$$

![](images/d8/d8821d28bf82000854b2181703a7daf3825b604211b4c136107a72a65f647c98.png)

- The permutation $\sigma_5$ maps $1,2,3$ to $3,1,2.$ So, we have

$$
\sigma_5(1) = 3, \quad \sigma_5(2) = 1, \quad \sigma_5(3)=2.
$$

![](images/8a/8af574ef3264b30640163411fe80e1a76bfc3b681274b993f05a5283f4bae80b.png)

- The permutation $\sigma_6$ maps $1,2,3$ to $3,2,1.$ So, we have

$$
\sigma_6(1) = 3, \quad \sigma_6(2) = 2, \quad \sigma_6(3)=1.
$$

![](images/e3/e3d19ac024e9b55b792495ef3cb0624d17e95e708f6df23b4a8dd0981f06b680.png)

**Watch out!** In the context of abstract algebra, a permutation is *not* just an ordering of numbers. Rather, a permutation is a *function* that maps some numbers from one ordering to another.

Permutations are often represented using a matrix of numbers, where the top row represents inputs to the permutation and the bottom row represents outputs from the permutation.

For example, consider the permutation $\sigma$ which maps $1,2,3$ to ${\color{blue}3},{\color{blue}1},{\color{blue}2}.$ We have that $\sigma(1) = {\color{blue}3},$ $\sigma(2) = {\color{blue}1},$ and $\sigma(3) = {\color{blue}2},$ and we write

$$
\sigma = {\left( \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{gray}↓} & {\color{gray}↓} & {\color{gray}↓} \\ \sigma  ( 1 ) & \sigma  ( 2 ) & \sigma  ( 3 )\end{array} \right)} = {\left( \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{gray}↓} & {\color{gray}↓} & {\color{gray}↓} \\ {\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2}\end{array} \right)} = {\left( \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2}\end{array} \right)}.
$$

Note that the columns of this matrix can be put in any order and still represent the same permutation. For example, 

$$
\sigma = {\left( \begin{array}{ccc}3 & 2 & 1 \\ {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}3}\end{array} \right)}.
$$

Then we still have $\sigma(3) = {\color{blue}2},$ $\sigma(2) = {\color{blue}1},$ and $\sigma(1) = {\color{blue}3}.$
